pages.text: BLM Invites Initial Public Feedback for April 2027 Oil and Gas Lease Sale in Ohio | Bureau of Land Management Skip to main navigation Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Press Releases BLM Invites Initial Public Feedback for April 2027 Oil and Gas Lease Sale in Ohio Organization: Bureau of Land Management Media Contact: BLM Eastern States Communications BLM_ES_News@BLM.gov Nov 10, 2026 An oil pump jack stands silhouetted against a sunset as the Bureau of Land Management opened a 30-day public scoping period today to receive public input on 20 oil and gas parcels totaling 824 acres that may be included in an April 2027 lease sale in Ohio. FALLS CHURCH, Va. – The Bureau of Land Management opened a 30-day public scoping period today to receive public input on 20 oil and gas parcels totaling 824 acres that may be included in an April 2027 lease sale in Ohio. The scoping period ends Dec. 10, 2026. Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources. Before development operations can begin, an operator must submit an application for permit to drill detailing development plans. The BLM reviews applications for permits to drill, posts them for public review, conducts an environmental analysis and coordinates with state partners and stakeholders. All parcels that are included in a federal oil and gas lease sale include appropriate stipulations to protect important natural resources. Information on current and upcoming BLM leases is available through the National Fluid Lease Sale System . BLM lease sales are held online through Efficient Markets . The parcels BLM is analyzing, as well as maps and instructions on how to comment, are available on the BLM’s ePlanning website at: https://eplanning.blm.gov/project-home/?id=51833F74-7BDC-F111-84E8-001DD8012CEA . The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

pages.description: IR-2026-128SP, 23 de octubre de 2026 — El Servicio de Impuestos Internos instó hoy a los contribuyentes a tomar medidas sencillas desde ahora para facilitar la presentación de sus declaraciones y evitar sorpresas durante la próxima temporada de impuestos.
pages.text: Recordatorio del IRS: La planificación tributaria durante todo el año puede facilitar la presentación de impuestos | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Recordatorio del IRS: La planificación tributaria durante todo el año puede facilitar la presentación de impuestos English Español Más en Noticias en Español Reducción de impuestos para las familias trabajadoras (en inglés) Notas de Prensa Notas de prensa para Preguntas frecuentes Alivio en situaciones de desastre Temas en las noticias Hojas de datos Declaraciones y anuncios del IRS Consejos tributarios del IRS Directrices del IRS (en inglés) Centro de medios Artículos sobre impuestos para compartir Pósteres para compartir IR-2026-128SP, 23 de octubre de 2026 WASHINGTON — El Servicio de Impuestos Internos (IRS, por sus siglas en inglés) instó hoy a los contribuyentes a tomar medidas sencillas desde ahora para facilitar la presentación de sus declaraciones y evitar sorpresas durante la próxima temporada de impuestos. La planificación tributaria a lo largo del año puede ayudar a los contribuyentes a mantenerse organizados, comprender cómo los cambios en su vida o en sus ingresos pueden afectar a sus impuestos, y prepararse para la temporada de presentación de impuestos. La Publicación 5349-A, Planificación tributaria durante todo el año: una guía para todos PDF , ofrece consejos prácticos y recursos del IRS para ayudar a los contribuyentes a lo largo del año. “Los contribuyentes deben planificar para garantizar que su temporada de presentación de impuestos transcurra de la manera más fluida posible”, señaló Frank J. Bisignano, director ejecutivo del IRS. “Tomar algunas medidas sencillas ahora —como revisar las retenciones, organizar los documentos, usar las herramientas en línea del IRS y proteger la información personal— ayudará a los contribuyentes a prepararse para la temporada de presentación de 2027 y a tener la tranquilidad de estar listos para cumplir con sus obligaciones tributarias”. Verifique las retenciones y los pagos de impuestos estimados Por lo general, los impuestos federales sobre los ingresos se pagan a lo largo del año a medida que se obtienen los ingresos. Los contribuyentes pueden usar la herramienta Estimador para retención de impuestos en IRS.gov para verificar si se les está reteniendo la cantidad correcta de impuestos federales sobre sus ingresos. Los contribuyentes deberían considerar revisar sus retenciones tras un cambio importante en su vida o en sus ingresos, como contraer matrimonio, divorciarse, el nacimiento o la adopción de un hijo, o un cambio de empleo. Aquellos que necesiten ajustar sus retenciones deben presentar un nuevo Formulario W-4 Certificado de retenciones del empleado a su empleador. Los contribuyentes que reciben ingresos no sujetos a retención —incluidos los propietarios de pequeñas empresas, los trabajadores por cuenta propia y quienes trabajan en la economía compartida— podrían necesitar realizar pagos trimestrales de impuestos estimados. Ciertos acontecimientos vitales también pueden influir en el estado civil tributario, la elegibilidad para recibir créditos y deducciones tributarias, y el monto de los impuestos a pagar o a recibir como reembolso. Revisar estos cambios antes de que comience la temporada de presentación de impuestos puede ayudar a los contribuyentes a comprender cómo podrían afectar a su declaración de impuestos federales sobre los ingresos. Aproveche las herramientas en línea del IRS Los contribuyentes pueden acceder de forma segura a su información tributaria y realizar muchas tareas habituales a través de la Cuenta en línea para individuos del IRS. Dependiendo de su cuenta, los contribuyentes pueden usarla para: Consultar el saldo de su cuenta Realizar y ver pagos Revisar planes de pago Ver determinados avisos y cartas del IRS Acceder a ciertos registros tributarios Solicitar un PIN de protección de la identidad (IP PIN) Los contribuyentes pueden visitar IRS.gov/Tools para encontrar recursos que les

pages.title: US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison submits Amanda Nunes to retain UFC title at MSG | UFC | The Guardian
pages.description: Kayla Harrison submitted Amanda Nunes in the fourth round at UFC 334, while Ciryl Gane edged Josh Hokit to retain his heavyweight championship
pages.text: US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison submits Amanda Nunes to retain UFC title at MSG | UFC | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Kayla Harrison celebrates after submitting Amanda Nunes to retain her UFC women’s bantamweight title at Madison Square Garden in New York on Saturday night. Photograph: Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC View image in fullscreen Kayla Harrison celebrates after submitting Amanda Nunes to retain her UFC women’s bantamweight title at Madison Square Garden in New York on Saturday night. Photograph: Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC UFC US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison submits Amanda Nunes to retain UFC title at MSG Two-time Olympic judo champion submits MMA legend Nunes falls short in return from three-year retirement Gane edges Hokit on points to retain heavyweight crown Agencies Sun 15 Nov 2026 00.31 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 03.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Kayla Harrison retained her UFC women’s bantamweight championship with a fourth-round submission of Amanda Nunes on Saturday night at Madison Square Garden, spoiling the comeback bid of the woman widely regarded as the greatest female fighter in MMA history. Harrison (20-1) had plenty to prove in her first title defense against Nunes, who ended a three-year retirement for the long-awaited showdown. It was also Harrison’s first fight since June 2025, after spinal fusion surgery in January to address a neck injury forced the postponement of the bout. Nunes (23-6) tried to wrestle with the two-time Olympic judo gold medalist and ended the first two rounds flat on her back. Harrison landed a series of short punches and elbows to the head that seemed to tire her out – she later acknowledged the difficulty of cutting weight to 135lb – as much as they damaged Nunes. Harrison, who walked out to Eye of the Tiger while the fighter known as the Lioness stretched and bounced on her tiptoes ahead of Bruce Buffer’s introductions, wasted no time in the fourth round. Harrison grabbed Nunes by her right leg and tripped her to the canvas before taking her back and applying a rear-naked choke. Nunes quickly tapped out, to the astonishment of the packed Garden crowd. “I think I’m still in shock,” Harrison said. Nunes may be considered the greatest fighter in the sport’s history. Harrison staked her claim as the best right now. Nunes walked out of the octagon on her own, while a victorious but weakened Harrison needed help returning to the locker room, championship belt firmly around her waist. “I’ve got a lot of decisions to make when I get home,” Harrison said. “Every time I make weight, I say never again, so we’ll see.” A UFC Hall of Famer, Nunes held championships in two weight classes, lost only once in 12 previous UFC title bouts and defeated the once-indomitable Ronda Rousey. She retired in 2023, citing burnout and a desire to spend more time with her wife as they raised their two young daughters. View image in fullscreen Kayla Harrison reacts after submitting Amanda Nunes in the fourth round to retain her UFC bantamweight title at Madison Square Garden in New York on Saturday night. Photograph: Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC She could return to retirement with her legacy as one of the sport’s greatest fighters secure. In the main event, Ciryl Gane successfully defended his heavyweight championship, sweeping the scorecards over the five-round fight to win a unanimous decision and beat Josh Hokit. Gane won 48-47 on all three scorecards as the pro-Hokit crowd howled in disbelief. Gane (15-2) defeated Alex Pereira at the White House card in June and claimed the interim heavyweight title before he was promoted to undisputed champion in Tom Aspinall’s absence November. Gane and Hokit (10-1) engaged in a slugfest that left both fighters bloodied – Hokit above the left eye, Gane from the mouth – but neither one landed any sustained offense which forced this outcome to the judges. pages.text: Raw Milk | FDA Skip to main content Skip to FDA Search Skip to in this section menu Skip to footer links Home Food Resources for You (Food) Raw Milk Resources for You (Food) In this section Los Riesgos de la Leche sin Pasteuriza Raw milk is milk from cows, sheep, or goats that has not been pasteurized to kill harmful bacteria. This raw, unpasteurized milk can carry dangerous bacteria such as Salmonella , E. coli , and Listeria , which are responsible for causing numerous foodborne illnesses. Decades ago, pasteurization of milk was adopted as a basic public health measure to kill dangerous bacteria. This measure largely eliminated the risk of getting sick from one of the most important staples of the American diet. pages.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial for deaths of her three children in March 2027 British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
pages.text: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial for deaths of her three children in March 2027 Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children 18 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ana Faguy Watch: Date announced for Lindsay Clancy retrial Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing. Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation. The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face. Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges. Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis. "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing. Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June. Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person. The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment. Plymouth Clerk's Office Clancy with her ex-husband and their children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning. A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy. Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction. The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury. Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out. It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked. The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility. The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US. Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. pages.description: Learn how a bill becomes a law, and how the process is different in the U.S. House of Representatives than in the U.S. Senate.
pages.text: How laws are made | USAGov Skip to main content How laws are made Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government. Learn how a bill becomes a law and how the process is different in the House of Representatives and in the Senate. How a bill becomes a law A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law. The idea for a bill can come from a: Sitting member of the U.S. Senate or House of Representatives Proposal during a congressional candidate's election campaign Petition by people or citizen groups who recommend a new or amended law to a member of Congress that represents them Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill. The bill is then put before that chamber to be voted on. If the bill passes one body of Congress, it goes to the other body to go through a similar process of research, discussion, changes, and voting. Once both bodies vote to accept a bill, they must work out any differences between the two versions. Then both chambers vote on the same version of the bill. If it passes, they present it to the president. The president then considers the bill. The president can approve the bill and sign it into law. Or the president can refuse to approve a bill. This is called a veto. If the president chooses to veto a bill, in most cases Congress can vote to override that veto and the bill becomes a law. But if the president does not sign off on a bill and it remains unsigned when Congress is no longer in session, the bill will be vetoed by default. This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress. Learn more about the U.S. Congress. How the House and Senate’s lawmaking procedures are different The Senate and the House have some procedural differences. While both are equal in how they function: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation Only the Senate can draft legislation related to presidential nominations and treaties While the House processes legislation through a majority vote, the Senate does so through deliberation and debate prior to voting. Información básica sobre la enfermedad del Ébola Para todos 10 de ago. del 2026 English (US) Puntos clave La enfermedad del Ébola es causada por una infección por un ortoebolavirus. Los ortoebolavirus se encuentran principalmente en África subsahariana. Los ortoebolavirus pueden causar una enfermedad grave y a menudo mortal, con una tasa de mortalidad tan alta como del 80 al 90 %. El ébola NO se propaga de la misma manera que los virus respiratorios como los de la influenza (gripe) y los del COVID-19. Usted no puede contraerlo por estar cerca de alguien. Lo que es Brote de ébola actual Vea las actualizaciones sobre el brote de ébola actual aquí . La enfermedad del Ébola es causada por un grupo de virus conocidos como ortoebolavirus (anteriormente llamados ebolavirus) 1 . Estos virus pueden causar una enfermedad grave que, sin tratamiento, puede causar la muerte. Los ortoebolavirus se descubrieron en 1976 en la República Democrática del Congo y se encuentran principalmente en África subsahariana. Proveedores de atención médica: Revisen las directrices sobre servicios de emergencia, evaluación, pruebas de detección, control de infecciones y equipo de protección personal (EPP) para las fiebres hemorrágicas virales, como la enfermedad del Ébola. Ver directrices sobre fiebres hemorrágicas virales Tipos Hay 4 tipos de ortoebolavirus que causan enfermedad entre las personas: El virus del Ébola (especie Orthoebolavirus zairense ) causa la enfermedad por el virus del Ébola. El virus de Sudán (especie Orthoebolavirus sudanense ) causa la enfermedad por el virus de Sudán. El virus del bosque Taï (especie Orthoebolavirus taiense ) causa la enfermedad por el virus del bosque Taï. El virus de Bundibugyo (especie Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense ) causa la enfermedad por el virus de Bundibugyo. Otras dos especies de ortoebolavirus no han afectado a personas hasta la fecha: El virus de Reston (especie Orthoebolavirus restonense ) ha causado enfermedad en primates no humanos como los macacos. El virus de Bombali (especie Orthoebolavirus bombaliense ) se identificó recientemente en murciélagos. Signos y síntomas Alguien con la enfermedad del Ébola podría empezar a sentirse enfermo entre 2 y 21 días después de tener contacto con un ortoebolavirus. Sin embargo, en promedio los síntomas aparecen 8 a 10 días después de la exposición. Las personas con la enfermedad del Ébola podrían presentar síntomas "secos" al principio del curso de la enfermedad. Estos síntomas pueden incluir fiebre, malestar, dolores y fatiga. Al enfermarse más la persona, por lo general, la enfermedad evoluciona hasta que se presentan síntomas "húmedos" que pueden incluir diarrea, vómitos y sangrado sin causa aparente. Seguir leyendo Signos y síntomas de la enfermedad del Ébola Factores de riesgo Los proveedores de atención médica y los familiares que cuidan a alguien con la enfermedad del Ébola sin usar métodos adecuados de control de infecciones tienen el riesgo más alto de infección. Los virus que causan la enfermedad del Ébola presentan poco riesgo para los viajeros o el público en general. Ampliar Descargar La enfermedad del Ébola es muy diferente del COVID-19. Cómo se propaga Las personas pueden contraer la enfermedad del Ébola a través del contacto con líquidos corporales de una persona infectada que esté enferma o haya muerto. Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us White Sands National Park: Following the Footprints White Sands National Park , in New Mexico, is extraordinary in many ways, but what truly sets it apart is its unparalleled record of coexistence among people, plants, and animals on this landscape during the late Pleistocene and early Holocene. What appears today as a dry playa or desolate salt flat was once a vibrant system of wetlands and lake margins. These ancient environments are partially restored only during rare, heavy rains that return water to the Tularosa Basin every few decades. At White Sands, scientists have identified more than 20 distinct sedimentary horizons, preserved over more than 10 vertical feet of sedimentary deposits, that record cycles of past water abundance as well as drought. Within these layers are remarkable trace fossils which have inspired the 2026 National Fossil Day artwork, including footprints of short-faced bears, large cats such as the American lion and saber-toothed cat, giant ground sloths, horses, and humans—providing rare insight into Ice Age life and interactions. Radiocarbon dating of these layers has revealed that people shared the land here with Pleistocene megafauna at least 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, making White Sands National Park the site of the oldest known human footprints in the region. Today, we understand that White Sands is not alone in preserving these incredible records. Instead, it serves as a powerful analog for other Ice Age pluvial lake systems that have since transformed into salt flats and desert playas across the southwest region of the United States. Treading New Ground The unique geology of White Sands created a depositional setting suitable for trace fossil preservation, many of which have now been revealed by years of research at the park which is primarily known for the world’s largest gypsum dunefield. Around 280 to 250 million years ago, towards the end of the Permian Period, a shallow sea covered much of what is now the southwestern United States. As sea level changed over time, evaporite minerals such as gypsum were sometimes deposited when water evaporated from shallow basins. Over millions of years gypsum accumulated in layers. Much later, the shifting of tectonic plates in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic Eras built the Rocky Mountains and created fault zones. Around 30 million years ago, the San Andreas and Sacramento Mountain ranges split due to tectonic activity, and the Tularosa Basin formed between them. The Rio Grande River brought sediments into the basin and water was trapped at the basin’s lowest point, eventually forming the ancient Lake Otero.During the Pleistocene, the climate fluctuated between warm and cold many times. When conditions were warm, snowmelt from the surrounding mountains carried dissolved gypsum into the lake basin. Eventually the lake would shrink after the snows melted, becoming a dry lakebed, or playa, like what is seen at White Sands today. One such warming period began following the end of the last Ice Age of the Late Pleistocene, around 12,000 years ago. The drier climate transformed the area into the modern Chihuahuan Desert, and selenite crystals formed on dry portions of the lakebed known as Alkali Flat. Winds broke down and polished the crystal grains into the characteristic white color of the dunes. Energy Department Announces New Partnership with NVIDIA and Oracle to Build Largest DOE AI Supercomputer The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), Argonne National Laboratory, NVIDIA and Oracle today announced a landmark public-private partnership to deliver the DOE’s largest AI supercomputer and accelerate scientific discovery. Energy.gov October 28, 2025 Estimated Read Time min WASHINGTON— The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), Argonne National Laboratory, NVIDIA and Oracle today announced a landmark public-private partnership to deliver the DOE’s largest AI supercomputer and accelerate scientific discovery. The partnership will also immediately deliver world-class AI computing resources to DOE researchers while simultaneously building two next-generation AI supercomputing systems at Argonne National Laboratory. Today’s announcement is in accordance with President Trump’s Executive Orders, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure and Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence . The Solstice system, which will feature 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, will be the largest AI supercomputer in the DOE’s lab complex. Another system, called Equinox, will feature 10,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Construction at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility will immediately begin for the Equinox system. It is expected to be delivered in 2026. These AI systems will be seamlessly connected with DOE’s vast network of scientific instruments and data assets to address some of the nation’s most pressing challenges in energy, security, and discovery science. As part of the partnership, Oracle will also immediately provide DOE with access to AI computing resources that use a combination of NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell architectures. Scientists from Argonne and across the country will have access to new AI capabilities to drive technological leadership for science and energy applications. “Winning the AI race requires new and creative partnerships that will bring together the brightest minds and industries American technology and science has to offer,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright . “The two Argonne systems and the collaboration between the Department of Energy, NVIDIA, and Oracle represent a new commonsense approach to computing partnerships. These systems will be a powerhouse for scientific and technological innovation. Thanks to President Trump, we’re bringing new computing capacity online faster than ever before and turning shared innovation into national strength.” “AI is the most powerful technology of our time, and science is its greatest frontier,” said Jensen Huang , founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with the Department of Energy and Oracle, we’re building an AI factory that will serve as America’s engine for discovery, giving researchers access to the most advanced AI infrastructure to drive progress across fields ranging from healthcare research to materials.” DOE has a long history of public-private partnerships that have provided American leadership in supercomputing for decades, and thanks to President Trump, the Energy Department is forging ahead with bold new partnerships. This latest collaboration exemplifies DOE’s new model, which enables shared investments and shared computing power between government and industry. Risk Management for Trichloroethylene (TCE) Additional Information Staff contact for TCE: TSCA Hotline: (202) 554-1404 Email: TCE.TSCA@epa.gov Gabriela Rossner: 202-565-2426 Public dockets for TCE: EPA-HQ-OPPT-2020-0642 ; EPA-HQ-OPPT-2016-0737 ; EPA-HQ-OPPT-2019-0500 Below is information on EPA actions under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) to manage the unreasonable risk from trichloroethylene (TCE) and protect public health. TCE is a volatile organic compound used mostly in industrial and commercial processes. Consumer uses include cleaning and furniture care products, arts and crafts spray coatings, and automotive care products like brake cleaners, and other consumer products. On this page: Managing Risks from TCE Opportunities for public and stakeholder engagement On other pages: Learn how EPA manages unreasonable risks from chemicals currently on the market . View a list of all chemicals undergoing risk evaluation, including docket numbers and agency points of contact . Managing Risks from TCE In December 2024, EPA issued a final rule regulating TCE. Read the final risk management rule for TCE . In May 2026, EPA postponed the effective date of the conditions attached to the TSCA section 6(g) exemptions in the 2024 rule until judicial review concludes, as described in the final TCE rule. Read the Federal Register Notice . In September 2025, EPA released an interim final rule extending the prohibition compliance date for two specific uses of TCE which would otherwise have been prohibited on September 15, 2025: the use of TCE as a processing aid in the manufacture of nuclear fuel, and the disposal of TCE to wastewater by processors of TCE and processors and industrial and commercial users of TCE as a processing aid. On October 14, 2026, EPA proposed to extend two compliance dates while keeping the TCE ban in place. The compliance date for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate, for industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid, and for associated disposal to wastewater would move from December 18, 2026, to December 31, 2027. The first step-down in the phase-out of TCE processing as an intermediate in HFC-134a manufacturing would move from June 7, 2027, to December 31, 2027. Interim workplace protections under the 2024 rule continue to apply during this period. Read the proposed rule and submit comments in docket EPA-HQ-OPPT-2026-7327 . FACT SHEET: Regulation of TCE Under TSCA. (pdf) (429.49 KB) COMPLIANCE GUIDE: A Guide to Complying with the 2024 TCE Regulation Under TSCA (pdf) (1.5 MB) Prohibitions EPA is prohibiting most uses of TCE, including TCE manufacture Processing for most commercial and all consumer products. This will protect most people who are likely to be exposed to TCE from uses covered by TSCA, including all consumers and workers in many sectors and many communities. Uses to be Phased Out Over a Longer Period A limited number of uses in the workplace will be phased out over a longer period. Those uses will only continue with required stringent worker protections in place. All TCE uses with longer phaseout timeframes will have worker safety requirements, such as a Workplace Chemical Protection Plan that includes an inhalation exposure limit. The final rule sets a different inhalation exposure limit for airborne TCE than was proposed. This change was made in response to public comments to ensure the limit is feasible to implement and monitor while still reducing risk. pages.title: A Tyrannosaur Ate a Feathery Meal—and It Was Frozen in Time | National Geographic
pages.description: Dinosaur poop—possibly from a juvenile T. rex or Nanotyrannus—containing feathers, bone fragments, and fish scales provides a look at a Cretaceous-era food web.
pages.text: A Tyrannosaur Ate a Feathery Meal—and It Was Frozen in Time | National Geographic SCIENCE A Tyrannosaur Ate a Feathery Meal—and It Was Frozen in Time Dinosaur poop—possibly from a juvenile T. rex or Nanotyrannus— containing feathers, bone fragments, and fish scales provides a look at a Cretaceous-era food web. Researchers analyzing a 66-million-year-old coprolite discovered preserved plumage and bones from an extinct, fish-eating aquatic bird. Jingmai O'Connor By Riley Black Published September 10, 2026 The little aquatic bird had no idea it had just eaten its last meal. Its stomach was still full of scaly fish when a hungry, feathery dinosaur scooped it up, snapping its jaws shut in a puff of plumage. After a shake and a swallow, the bird slid down the predator’s throat. From there, most of it journeyed into the carnivore’s core to be broken down and folded into the creature’s own tissues. The remainder was excreted as dino dung. Now, some 66 million years later, researchers have found a feather and the gut contents from that bird preserved in the dinosaur’s fossilized poop. The coprolite, as paleontologists call it, contains a Cretaceous food web from just before the asteroid strike and adds a new wrinkle to the story of which birds survived and which went extinct. “This is the first fossil feather found in a coprolite,” says Jingmai O’Connor, a paleontologist at the Field Museum in Chicago. She and her colleagues published their findings Thursday in the journal Cu r r e nt Biology . ( How an Unlikely Fossil Hunter Found a Tyrannosaurus Trail ) Known by its catalog number "UWBM 103150," the fossilized feces consist of three rocky globs. It was likely expelled by a medium-sized carnivorous dinosaur that lived in Montana, perhaps a juvenile Ty r annosau r us r e x or the mini-tyrant Nanoty r annus . The lithified plops are flecked with tiny pieces of bone that best match a group of flightless, toothed birds called hesperornithiformes , which swam in prehistoric seas. “The preservation is truly amazing, almost as if it was in amber,” says Matthew Shawkey, a paleontologist from Ghent University in Belgium, who was not involved in the research. Eve r y dinosau r cop r olite is like a time capsule. The dung often contains tatters of the dinosaur’s most recent meal. Duck-billed dinosaurs, hungry for essential nutrients to form their eggs, munched on rotting logs filled with tiny invertebrates. Scientists found wood and exoskeletons in their droppings. An eight-inch-long scat attributed to T. r e x was found to contain bone fragments and even undigested pieces of muscle. “Since bits of bone pass through large theropod digestive systems, it’s not unsurprising that whole small feathers also pass through,” O’Connor says. Dinosaurs had elevated body temperatures and fast metabolisms, features associated with a quicker digestive system. That means that not everything they guzzled down was digested into nothingness, giving feathers a chance to make it through whole. Despite seeming fragile, feathers are made of a tough and fibrous material called keratin. ( How dinosau r vomit has solved these p r e histo r ic myste r ies ) SCIENCE Nanotyrannus likely was a tiny adult dino and not a teen T. rex SCIENCE Was Nanotyrannus real? SCIENCE Is it a bird? A monkey? No, it's a new prehistoric reptile “Very, very few animals are able to digest keratin, so it is reasonable to expect that feathers might be common in feces,” says Karen Chin, a paleontologist at the University of Colorado and an author on the study. A prehistoric dinosaur, likely a juvenile T. rex or a nanotyrannus , ate a small loon-like bird and then pooped out its remains. Some 66 million years later, scientists found a feather inside its fossilized feces. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Press Releases BLM Invites Additional Public Feedback for March 2027 Oil and Gas Lease Sale in Five Eastern States Organization: Bureau of Land Management BLM Office: Eastern States State Office Media Contact: BLM Eastern States Communications blm_es_news@blm.gov Nov 9, 2026 An oil pump jack stands silhouetted against a sunset as the Bureau of Land Management opened a 30-day public comment period today to receive public input on plans to include 15 oil and gas parcels in five Eastern States, including Alabama, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, and Ohio, totaling approximately 2,830 acres, in a March 2027 sale. FALLS CHURCH, Va. – The Bureau of Land Management opened a 30-day public comment period today to receive public input on plans to include 15 oil and gas parcels in five Eastern States, including Alabama, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, and Ohio, totaling approximately 2,830 acres, in a March 2027 sale. The comment period ends Dec. 9. The BLM completed scoping on these parcels in July and is now seeking public comment on the parcels and related environmental analysis. The BLM will use input from the public to help complete its review of each parcel. Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources. Before development operations can begin, an operator must submit an application for permit to drill detailing development plans. The BLM reviews applications for permits to drill, posts them for public review, conducts an environmental analysis and coordinates with state partners and stakeholders. All parcels that are included in a federal oil and gas lease sale include appropriate stipulations to protect important natural resources. Information on current and upcoming BLM leases is available through the National Fluid Lease Sale System . BLM lease sales are held online through Efficient Markets . The parcels BLM is analyzing, as well as maps and instructions on how to comment, are available on the BLM’s ePlanning website at: Split Estate EOls in Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier Parish, Louisiana Conecuh NF Expressions of Interest Jackson County, Michigan Monroe County, Ohio The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

pages.description: Trump has long relied on sports to project strength and fuel his culture wars. But after a crushing midterm defeat, even his UFC ally cannot distract from the political fallout
pages.text: Trump’s pathetic Dana White gambit could not mask his midterm humiliation | UFC | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Donald Trump and UFC president Dana White walk onto the South Lawn of the White House ahead of the UFC Freedom 250 event in Washington DC. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Donald Trump and UFC president Dana White walk onto the South Lawn of the White House ahead of the UFC Freedom 250 event in Washington DC. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images UFC Trump’s pathetic Dana White gambit could not mask his midterm humiliation Howard Bryant Trump has long relied on sports to project strength and fuel his culture wars. But after a crushing midterm defeat, even his UFC ally cannot distract from the political fallout Mon 9 Nov 2026 05.00 EST Last modified on Mon 9 Nov 2026 22.40 EST Share I n the wake of being destroyed in the midterm elections , it was only a matter of time before Donald Trump did something outrageous in an attempt to misdirect public attention away from his catastrophic losses. Before the midterms, published reports suggested the possibility of apocalypse, global or domestic – a nuclear strike on Iran, martial law to suspend last week’s elections, the invalidation of individual races, such as in Alaska – but Trump opted for banality over Armageddon, offering his vacant press secretary opening to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White. It was absurd, and widely posited that a confused Trump had erroneously conflated UFC’s White with the Dana White who made more sense, former Heritage Foundation staffer Dana White. Because the public reactions made him look even more lost, confirming the sentiments of recklessness and disorder, utter chaos and buffoonery that led to the Republicans being routed in the midterm elections, the president said his offer to White was all a joke . As a disciple of the notorious McCarthyite Roy Cohn, who taught Trump one of his main political pillars – never apologize or admit wrongdoing. Ever. – Trump should not, of course, be taken at his word. From ‘human cockfighting’ to the White House lawn: the stratospheric rise of the UFC’s Dana White Read more Either by mixing up the female PR professional Dana White with the UFC ringleader and having to backtrack regardless, Trump’s bluster has at last been pierced by last week’s mandate that a larger segment of the electorate is no longer charmed by his garrulousness, or energized by his ugly charisma. The downward spiral has begun. His press secretary job is vacant because his last choice, Katie Zacharia, lasted less than a week . Failure can only mean that Trump will intensify his worst instincts and play the hits that have always worked, in the arenas with the most eyeballs. 0:51 Donald Trump ‘kidding’ about making UFC boss Dana White US press secretary – video One of those arenas has always been sports, and thus it tracks that, joke or not, he would use White to wring another bit of life out of a news cycle. When Trump has needed headlines or kindling, he has turned to sports. He used the public’s always bizarre adulation and resentment toward Black athletes a decade ago by attacking Colin Kaepernick and the NFL, and sports has stood at the center of his culture wars ever since. He and his justice department have pivoted from the NFL to the NBA, waded into MLB by trying to turn Pride Night into an anti-Christian grievance. The WNBA now lives in his crosshairs. Trump relied on sports giving him the real-man boost and muscularity he always craves, but this time the gambit failed Trump has always relied on sports to bail him out. In trying to appeal to the machismo of his base and give America’s 250th birthday a performative sheen of strength, Trump held a UFC cage match on the White House South Lawn earlier this June – an event that was highlighted by one of White’s fighters racially insulting former first lady Michelle Obama . Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/bioinformatics Bioinformatics Sign Up to Get NIST News GovDelivery Bioinformatics plays a crucial role in advancing NIST's mission by computationally analyzing large amounts of complex biological data generated by NIST and its collaborators. NIST provides benchmarks for the computational tools and methodologies necessary for conducting such work. Omics (genomic, proteomic, metabolomic, metagenomic, and transcriptomic) data, generated both inside and outside of NIST, NIST’s reference materials, benchmark datasets, and metadata standards underpin biological research and innovation. These standards help ensure the accuracy and reliability of large-scale biological measurements, which is essential for fields such as engineering biology, precision medicine, biotechnology, and public health. The NIST-hosted Genome in a Bottle Consortium has developed authoritatively characterized human genome reference materials. As the first RMs to be characterized for billions of properties, these have been used to train and test AI-based models and other bioinformatics tools. Similarly, the NIST Genome Editing Program , including the public-private partnership NIST Genome Editing Consortium , is developing benchmark samples, control datasets, and metadata norms, and conducting interlaboratory studies to qualify bioinformatics tools and approaches used to detect intended and unintended genome edits which is essential information for clinical applications. Further work in this area includes onboarding and deploying systematic approaches to add confidence to computational pipelines and their outputs for measurements used to identify where genome editing technologies may have made unintended (off-target) changes in a genome. NIST’s Microbial Metrology Program develops advanced measurements, reference materials, and standards for microbial systems to promote human health, precision medicine, advanced manufacturing, and other industrial applications. The Cellular Engineering Group is developing predictable and versatile RNA circuits, based on nucleic acid strand displacement reactions to meet emerging molecular computation and measurement needs in biological systems. The NIST Mass Spectrometry Data Center develops evaluated mass spectral libraries and provides related software tools. Signos y síntomas de la enfermedad del Ébola Para todos 26 de may del 2026 English (US) Puntos clave Los síntomas de la enfermedad del Ébola aparecen de 2 a 21 días después de que alguien está expuesto al virus. Los síntomas "secos", como la fiebre y la debilidad, se presentan primero y pueden avanzar a síntomas "húmedos", como diarrea y vómitos. Debido a que sus síntomas no son específicos, la enfermedad del Ébola puede confundirse con enfermedades infecciosas más comunes. Síntomas iniciales Los síntomas de la enfermedad del Ébola pueden aparecer de 2 a 21 días después del contacto con el virus. En promedio, las personas comienzan a mostrar síntomas de 8 a 10 días después de la exposición. Al principio, los síntomas son genéricos y se conocen como síntomas "secos". Síntomas “secos” Fiebre Malestares y dolores en los músculos y las articulaciones Dolor de cabeza intenso Debilidad y fatiga Dolor de garganta Los proveedores de atención médica pueden confundir la enfermedad del Ébola con otras enfermedades infecciosas más comunes, como las siguientes: Malaria (paludismo) Influenza (gripe) Fiebre tifoidea Enfermedad meningocócica Otras infecciones bacterianas, como neumonía Síntomas posteriores Después de cuatro a cinco días de estar enfermos, los pacientes pueden avanzar a presentar síntomas "húmedos" a medida que se sienten más enfermos. Síntomas "húmedos" Pérdida del apetito Sangrado sin causa aparente Síntomas gastrointestinales Náuseas Dolor abdominal Diarrea Vómitos Otros síntomas Otros síntomas pueden incluir dolor en el pecho, dificultad para respirar, confusión, ojos enrojecidos, sarpullido, hipo y convulsiones. Dato Los pacientes que fallecen por la enfermedad del Ébola, por lo general presentan más síntomas graves al inicio de la enfermedad. Los pacientes que sobreviven podrían tener fiebre varios días y empezar a mejorarse unos 6 días después de que los síntomas empezaron. Complicaciones y cuándo buscar ayuda Los sobrevivientes de la enfermedad del Ébola podrían tener complicaciones a largo plazo, como las siguientes: Cansancio Dolores de cabeza Dolor en los músculos y las articulaciones Problemas de los ojos y la vista (visión borrosa, dolor, enrojecimiento, sensibilidad a la luz) Aumento de peso Dolor de estómago o falta de apetito Otros problemas de salud pueden incluir pérdida de la memoria, hinchazón del cuello, boca seca, opresión en el pecho, pérdida del cabello, problemas auditivos, dolor u hormigueo en las manos y los pies, inflamación de los tejidos que rodean al corazón, inflamación de uno o ambos testículos, cambios en la menstruación, impotencia, disminución o pérdida del interés sexual, dificultar para dormir o permanecer dormidos, depresión, ansiedad y trastorno de estrés postraumático (PTSD, por sus siglas en inglés). El momento de la aparición, la gravedad y la duración de las complicaciones varía entre los sobrevivientes de la enfermedad del Ébola. Cuándo buscar ayuda Si usted cree que estuvo expuesto a alguien con la enfermedad del Ébola y está presentando signos y síntomas de la enfermedad del Ébola, comuníquese con su médico o departamento de salud estatal inmediatamente. pages.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
pages.text: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? 22 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Faisal Islam , Economics editor and Lucy Hooker , Business reporter Getty Images Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland. Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”. It has been this way since Brexit. Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays. It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021. Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped. All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade. That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday. The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households. But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make? EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made. In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies. The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker. But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules. Exit clause A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. The reset means they will be dismantled. Getty Images The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves". He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. How EPA Evaluates the Safety of Existing Chemicals Overview The Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), as amended by the Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21 st Century Act, requires EPA to evaluate the safety of existing chemicals via a three-stage process. The three stages of EPA’s process for ensuring the safety of existing chemicals are prioritization, risk evaluation, and risk management. The statute also includes a variety of new EPA authorities to drive forward progress on evaluating and ensuring the safety of existing chemicals. The following graphic provides an overview of the process for prioritization, risk evaluation and risk management of existing chemicals, including the key decisions to be made or actions taken at each step: Once a chemical is in the process, which starts with proposed prioritization of a chemical, statutory deadlines are triggered for EPA to complete each stage of the process: Prioritization Risk evaluation Risk management Prioritization The first step in EPA’s process for evaluating the safety of existing chemicals is prioritization. Prioritization is a risk-based screening process for designating chemical substances as either High-Priority Substances for risk evaluation, or Low-Priority Substances for which risk evaluation is not warranted at the time. TSCA requires EPA to give certain preferences to prioritizing chemicals on the 2014 TSCA Work Plan , to consider certain criteria such as hazard/exposure, persistence and bioaccumulation, but otherwise does not significantly limit EPA's discretion to choose which chemicals enter the prioritization process. TSCA further prohibits EPA from considering non-risk factors (e.g., costs/benefits) during prioritization. Once initiated, the process provides stakeholders with ample notice of any EPA risk evaluation activity, as well as two opportunities for the public to submit relevant information to the Agency. The process has been designed to ensure that the Agency’s limited resources are focused on chemicals with the greatest potential for risk. Chemical substances with low hazard and/or exposure that meet the definition of Low-Priority Substances are taken out of consideration for further assessment at this time. This gives the public notice of chemical substances for which the hazard and/or exposure potential is anticipated to be low or nonexistent, and provides insight into which chemical substances are likely not to need additional evaluation and risk management. Learn more about EPA’s process for prioritizing existing chemicals for risk evaluation . Risk Evaluation The second step in EPA’s process for evaluating the safety of existing chemicals is risk evaluation. If EPA designates a chemical as a High-Priority Substance, the chemical moves immediately to the risk evaluation phase. At the conclusion of the risk evaluation phase, EPA must use the risk evaluation as a basis to determine whether or not the chemical presents an unreasonable risk to health or the environment under the chemical’s conditions of use. TSCA prohibits EPA from considering non-risk factors (e.g., costs/benefits) during risk evaluation. This includes risks to subpopulations who may be at greater risks than the general population, such as children and workers. pages.text: The Echoes of Toothed Birds | National Geographic Photo by Brian Switek. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. It takes an encyclopedic knowledge of anatomy to spot the differences, but the bones don’t lie. For example, as pointed out by Natural History Museum of Los Angeles paleontologists Alyssa Bell and Luis Chiappe in their new paper on Hesperornis and kin, loons, grebes, and the toothed birds all evolved different skeletal scaffolds for increasing their swimming power. Grebes have an expansion of the tibia for strong propulsive muscles, while loons split the space between a flange on their tibia and a kneecap. In the extinct toothed birds, however, the muscles mainly appear to have attached to a large, robust kneecap. Different anatomical solutions to the same mechanical problem. The family tree of hesperornithiform birds created by Bell and Chiappe, 2015. From differences such as these, paleontologists have been able to discern that the hesperornithiformes are perched just outside the “modern” bird group – Neornithes to specialists – on the avian family tree. So far, so good. But as Bell and Chiappe point out in their paper, very little work has been done on sorting out the relationships of the various diving birds that snatched fish with snaggly jaws among the Northern Hemishphere’s Cretaceous waterways. With that in mind, the researchers cataloged 207 skeletal characteristics from 272 hesperornithiform specimens representing 18 different taxa to see who was related to whom. After the various lineages grew or were pruned, Bell and Chiappe found that all the hesperornithiform birds created one group, and under this canopy there were several major branches. This is what allowed Bell and Chiappe to see how these birds became better and better adapted to lives spent at sea. Over time, the researchers point out, the birds show increasing specializations for better diving – such as a close connection of bone in the lower leg that allowed Hesperornis and other skilled swimmers to hold their toes close together during the recovery phase of a swim stroke, reducing drag and allowing them to get their feet in position for the next sweep faster. Not that the story is one of straight-line progress from little flappy birds to flightless divers. Looking across the lineages, Bell and Chiappe found that these toothed birds evolved large body size at least three different times – in species of Brodavis and Pasquiaornis , as well as Hesperornis and its closest relatives. This might be a sign that each of these lineages were independently becoming adapted to being better divers. Bigger body size in diving animals, Bell and Chiappe poin

Energy Department Announces $134 Million to Advance U.S. Fusion Leadership Through Targeted Research The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced $134 million in funding for two programs designed to secure U.S. leadership in emerging fusion technologies and innovation. Energy.gov September 10, 2025 Estimated Read Time min Funding for the next round of Fusion Innovation Research Engine (FIRE) Collaboratives and the Innovation Network for Fusion Energy (INFUSE) awards will enhance connections between private fusion industry, DOE national labs, and universities WASHINGTON— The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced $134 million in funding for two programs designed to secure U.S. leadership in emerging fusion technologies and innovation. These investments are part of DOE’s broader mission to unleash American energy, science, and innovation, ensuring the technologies that define the future of fusion power are developed here in the United States. “Under President Trump’s leadership, DOE is unleashing the next frontier of American energy,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright . “Fusion power holds the promise of limitless, reliable, American-made energy—and programs like INFUSE and FIRE ensure our innovators have the tools, talent, and partnerships to make it a reality.” DOE is announcing $128 million for the Fusion Innovative Research Engine (FIRE) collaboratives. The funding was awarded to seven teams that are focused on creating a fusion energy science and technology innovation ecosystem by forming virtual, centrally managed teams. The teams selected have a collective goal of bridging the DOE Fusion Energy Sciences (FES) program’s basic science research programs and growing fusion industries. DOE is also announcing $6.1 million in funding for the Innovation Network for Fusion Energy (INFUSE) program. With this funding, DOE has selected 20 projects that accelerate private-sector fusion energy development by reducing barriers to collaboration between businesses and national laboratories or universities. The projects selected include research in materials science, laser technology development, high temperature superconducting magnet assessment, artificial intelligence (AI) learning for fusion modeling and simulation, and enabling technologies to move toward achieving economical fusion energy. Fusion has the potential to provide abundant, reliable energy by replicating the same process that powers the sun and stars. Following the passage of the Energy Act of 2020, FES has sought to accelerate the viability of commercial fusion energy in partnership with the private sector by establishing several industry-relevant programs like INFUSE and the FIRE Collaboratives. These initiatives represent a significant step forward in advancing fusion energy research, maintaining U.S. leadership in fusion, strengthening U.S. based manufacturing and supply chains and supporting the development of technologies crucial for national security, energy security, and defense. In accordance with President Trump's recent executive order Unleashing American Energy , these selections advance domestic fusion production and expand collaboration across the growing American fusion industry. A full list of projects and additional information can be found on the Fusion Energy Sciences program homepage . Background on INFUSE : INFUSE solicited proposals from the fusion industry and selected projects for one-year awards. The selected projects ranging between $100,000 and $500,000 each were selected through a competitive peer review

pages.text: blackadder's Diary | Bicycle woes | OpenStreetMap Select Language Loading... Close blackadder's Diary Bicycle woes Posted by blackadder on 9 May 2007 in English . In order of preference my bike is far more productive for mapping urban areas than the car or on foot. So when both my bikes get sick I'm kind of at a bit of a loss to know what to do. Clearly I should spend time fixing the puncture and broken spoke but that requires me to get my hands dirty so perhaps best left till the weekend. Still, got some mapping in yesterday around Kings Bromley as well as some more street mapping in Erdington on Monday and a little canal towpath coverage along the Coventry canal on Sunday. That's what probably did the spoke in! Discussion Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Events & Meetings Wild Horse and Burro Adoption Event in Texarkana, Arkansas Eastern States Southeastern States DO Event Coordinator Lindsay Rasmussen Lrasmussen@blm.gov (601) 966-7686 BLM Office: Southeastern States Event Dates Nov 19, 2026 8:00 am CST to Nov 21, 2026 12:00 pm CST November 19, 2026, 8:00 am – 4:30 pm EST November 20, 2026, 8:00 am – 4:30 pm EST Event Location 3700 E. 50th Street Texarkana , AR 71854 United States Get Directions Event Description The Bureau of Land Management will host a wild horse and burro placement event, offering excess horses and burros gathered from western rangelands, November 19-20, 2026, at the Four States Fair in Texarkana, AR. “The BLM has placed over 300,000 wild horses and burros into private care since 1971,” said acting Southeastern States District Manager Shayne Banks. “This is an opportunity to provide a good home to one of America’s Living Legends.” The event will be open to the public November 19-20 from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. BLM staff will be onsite to provide more information and assist with the application process. To qualify to purchase a wild horse or burro: Applicants must be able to provide humane care for any animals purchased from the BLM. Applicants must agree they will not knowingly sell or transfer ownership of them to any person or organization that intends to resell, trade, or give away such animals for slaughter or processing into commercial products. To qualify to adopt a wild horse or burro: Applicants must be at least 18 years old with no record of animal abuse. Homes must have a minimum of 400 square feet of corral space per animal, with access to food, water, and shelter. Corral fence must meet height requirements: Adult horses - 6 feet, Yearlings - 5 feet, Burros – 4.5 feet Trailers must be stock type, covered, with swing gates and sturdy walls/floors. To learn more about BLM’s Wild Horse and Burro program, visit https://www.blm.gov/whb . Published on: October 9, 2026 The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

NIST's measurement methods and reference materials accelerate the development of lab-made materials that can help heal wounds or replace missing tissues, or be used to mimic human tissues for diagnostics or research. Our long partnership with the American Dental Association boasts advances such as the tooth-colored composites used to fill cavities and repair chipped teeth and the panoramic dental X-ray. The NIST Tissue Engineering project characterizes scaffolds, the supports used to "grow" replacement tissues, and the interactions between scaffolds and cells. Other work develops sensors that measure biological properties and the interactions of cells and materials. NIST also participates in the Multi-Agency Tissue Engineering Science coordination group. Cómo se propaga la enfermedad del Ébola Para todos 2 de jun. del 2026 English (US) Puntos clave Las personas y animales, incluso los primates, pueden infectarse por un virus que causa la enfermedad del Ébola proveniente de un animal portador. Las personas también pueden contraer la enfermedad del Ébola a través del contacto con líquidos corporales de una persona infectada o con objetos contaminados. Aun después de que alguien se recupere de la enfermedad del Ébola, el virus puede permanecer en áreas del cuerpo ocultas del sistema inmunitario. El ébola NO se propaga de la misma manera que los virus respiratorios como los de la influenza (gripe) y los del COVID-19. Usted no puede contraerlo por estar cerca de alguien. ¿Cuál es la causa? La enfermedad del Ébola es causada por un grupo de virus conocidos como ortoebolavirus. Cómo se propaga Entre los animales Los científicos creen que los murciélagos de la fruta africanos tienen un papel en la propagación de los ortoebolavirus. Estos murciélagos de la fruta podrían ser la fuente del virus. Los animales infectados pueden propagar el virus a otros animales a través del contacto con líquidos corporales infectados o artículos contaminados con estos líquidos. ¿Sabía usted? Cuando un animal infectado propaga el virus a una persona, se llama un salto interespecífico . Entre las personas Después del salto interespecífico inicial, el virus puede propagarse de persona a persona. Una persona se infecta cuando su piel abierta o las membranas mucosas en los ojos, la nariz o la boca entran en contacto con lo siguiente: La sangre o los líquidos corporales de una persona enferma o que murió a causa de la enfermedad del Ébola. Los líquidos corporales incluyen orina, saliva, sudor, heces, vómitos, leche materna y líquido amniótico. Objetos contaminados con los líquidos corporales de una persona enferma o que murió a causa de la enfermedad del Ébola. Esto puede incluir ropa, ropa de cama, agujas y equipo médico. Animales infectados, como los murciélagos, primates o antílopes de bosque. Estos virus se podrían propagar a través de la caza o la manipulación de animales infectados o su consumo. El semen de una persona que se recuperó de la enfermedad del Ébola. Esto puede ocurrir a través de las relaciones sexuales orales, vaginales o anales. No hay evidencia de que los ortoebolavirus se propagan a través del contacto con las secreciones vaginales de alguien que haya tenido la enfermedad del Ébola. El ébola no se propaga de la misma manera que los virus respiratorios como los de la influenza (gripe) y los del COVID-19. Usted no puede contraer el ébola por estar cerca de alguien. Dato No hay evidencia de que los mosquitos u otros insectos puedan propagar los virus que causan la enfermedad del Ébola. Ampliar Descargar La enfermedad del Ébola se propaga entre los animales y después da el salto a las personas. Cuándo es posible la transmisión Las personas con la enfermedad del Ébola pueden propagar el virus a otras cuando empiezan a tener síntomas. Las personas con ébola no pueden propagar la enfermedad antes de que los síntomas comiencen a aparecer. Algunos sobrevivientes de la enfermedad del Ébola todavía son portadores del virus. Gracias a los avances en los tratamientos más personas están sobreviviendo a la enfermedad del Ébola. Algunas personas que sobreviven a la enfermedad del Ébola pueden propagar el virus aun después de que desaparezcan los síntomas. Esto ocurre cuando el virus permanece en ciertas par

Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us Return to The Civil War Series: Prehistoric Life of Tule Springs Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument preserves thousands of Pleistocene (Ice Age) fossils that help tell the story of an ever-changing ecosystem. These fossils were preserved within expanding and contracting wetlands between 100,000-12,500 years ago. Many of the Pleistocene animals of Tule Springs are still alive today, including the coyote ( Canis latrans ), jackrabbit ( Lepus sp.), and aquatic snails. Some animals went extinct, disappearing from North America entirely. Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 1: Columbian Mammoth The Columbian mammoth is the largest and most identified extinct large mammal found in the Las Vegas Formation at Tule Springs Fossil Bed National Monument. Columbian mammoths belonged to the same family as living elephants. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 2: The Big Cats During the late Pleistocene, Tule Springs Fossil Beds was home to two extinct large cats: the sabertooth cat and the American lion. These apex predators represent two distinct cat lineages; one of which was the last of its kind in North America. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 3: The Camels Two different genera of camelids have been identified from the late Pleistocene deposits of Tule Springs. Fossils of the ancient camel make up one third (about 38%) of the total large Pleistocene mammals identified at Tule Springs. The ancient llama is only known from one fossil specimen. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 4: Ancient Horse Horses first evolved in North America during the Eocene epoch and adapted to the changing climate over tens of millions of years. Equus scotti was one of the last of the native North American horses and had a wide distribution over the continent, before it went extinct 10,000 years ago. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 5: Giant Ground Sloths Two species of giant ground sloth are represented in the Pleistocene fossil record of Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument: the Shasta ground sloth and Jefferson’s ground sloth. These extinct herbivores were approximately the size of a car. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 6: Dire Wolf The dire wolf is a recent addition to the Pleistocene fauna found at Tule Springs Fossil Beds. The dire wolf was about the size of the largest gray wolves, with a shoulder height of about three feet. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 7: Teratorn Approximately one-third larger than the California condor, the teratorn was the largest bird found at Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument. This scavenging raptor also hunted small mammals and had a 12-foot wingspan. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 8: Tule Springs Pronghorn Pronghorn fossils are known from Tule Springs Fossil Beds but none of them allow for identification to species. There are several candidates for which type of pronghorn lived in the Las Vegas Valley during the Pleistocene. Read more Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument Article 9: Ancient Bison Although some species have gone extinct, bison have lived in North America for hundreds of thousands of years. Herds of now-extinct bison once lived in what is now Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument during the Pleistocene epoch, between 100,000-12,500 years ago. pages.title: How dinosaur vomit has solved these prehistoric mysteries | National Geographic
pages.description: A new pterosaur species was recently discovered in the vomit of a dino. But that's just the start of revelations from prehistoric excretions.
pages.text: How dinosaur vomit has solved these prehistoric mysteries | National Geographic SCIENCE How dinosaur vomit has solved these prehistoric mysteries A new pterosaur species was recently discovered in the vomit of a dino. But that's just the start of revelations from prehistoric excretions. Millions of years ago, a predator like spinosaurus (shown in the background of this artist's illustration) ate the filter-feeding pterosaur Barikibu waridza, and then puked up its meal, which later fossilized. Julio Lacerda By Riley Black Published December 8, 2025 One day 110 million years ago, in what’s now Brazil, a dinosaur had to get something off its chest. Small, pokey bones had massed inside the animal’s digestive tract, getting in the way of munching on fish and other snacks. The carnivore voided the stinky lump from its throat, just like modern owls jettison pellets of massed bone and hair from their small prey. Sediment eventually covered the blob. It fossilized and was encapsulated in stone until it was recently uncovered by paleontologists. Inside were the bones of a flying reptile no one had even seen before. Time spent in the jaws and digestive system of a meat-eating creature was not kind to its meal’s skeleton. Despite their rough journey into the fossil record, however, the bones (mostly jaws and teeth) were well-preserved enough to tell they belonged to an unexpected species of pterosaur that sieved ancient waters for tiny creatures much the way flamingos do today. Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte paleontologist Aline Ghilardi and her colleagues named the pterosaur Bakiribu waridza when they described the find earlier this year . “This was not just a fossil concretion containing a new species of a rare type of pterosaur, but an exceptional ichnofossil, a regurgitalite,” Ghilardi says. Regurgitalites and other fossils of digestive contents fall under a broader category of fossils called bromalites. While they might sound gross, excreted masses cast off by dinosaurs and other prehistoric organisms offer direct insight into what living things were eating, how their internal organs work, and how long-lost species actually interacted with each other in ancient ecosystems. Is it porridge or a pterosaur? In the case of Bakiribu , the pterosaur’s discovery was fortuitous. “When my student William first showed me the concretion and asked what it was, I had an unusual stroke of luck,” Ghilardi says. She had just been reading about Pterodaustro , a pterosaur found in the rocks of Argentina and Chile with jaws of thin, closely-packed teeth that allowed the flier to filter-feed in prehistoric ponds. The jaws in the concretion looked very similar, only in a very different place. No pterosaur like this had been found in rocks of the same age within Brazil before. Ghilardi and colleagues immediately knew that the bones represented something new. Found in Brazil's Araripe Basin, this fossilized regurgitate contained a new pterosaur species amid some fish bones Aline Ghilardi But why did the bones look so messy? “I joked that it looked like someone had spot out a kind of porridge, and ‘Mingau,’” meaning porridge in Portuguese, “quickly became the fossils nickname,” Ghilardi says. While fossils are sometimes found within concretions that form after burial, layers of rock layering around a central nucleus of tooth or bone, Mingau was something else. The fragmented nature of the bones, the fish fossils, and the closely-packed nature of the remains indicated that the mass had been ejected from a larger animal—likely a predatory dinosaur. “It’s definitely an unusual pathway to take and end up as a fossil,” says University of Tennessee Knoxville paleontologist Stephanie Drumheller-Horton , who was not involved with the study. Mouch Jr Multi-Purpose Facility in Port Allen, LA. “The BLM has placed over 300,000 wild horses and burros into private care since 1971,” said Acting Southeastern States District Manager Shayne Banks. “This is an opportunity to provide a good home to one of America’s Living Legends.” The event will be open to the public October 15-16 from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and October 17, 8 a.m. to 12 p.m. BLM staff will be onsite to provide more information and assist with the application process. To qualify to purchase a wild horse or burro: Applicants must be able to provide humane care for any animals purchased from the BLM. Applicants must agree they will not knowingly sell or transfer ownership of them to any person or organization that intends to resell, trade, or give away such animals for slaughter or processing into commercial products. To qualify to adopt a wild horse or burro: Applicants must be at least 18 years old with no record of animal abuse. Homes must have a minimum of 400 square feet of corral space per animal, with access to food, water, and shelter. Corral fence must meet height requirements: Adult horses - 6 feet, Yearlings - 5 feet, Burros – 4.5 feet Trailers must be stock type, covered, with swing gates and sturdy walls/floors. To learn more about BLM’s Wild Horse and Burro program, visit https://www.blm.gov/whb . Related Files Port Allen, LA WHB Animal Shipping Report (PDF / 109 KB) Published on: October 4, 2026 The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.
