Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Cultivating Stewards: ICC Crews and Interns Transform Idaho’s Public Lands in 2026 Aug 21, 2026 This summer, students with the Idaho Conservation Corps (ICC) completed critical projects on BLM Idaho lands while gaining hands-on experience in land management and becoming stewards of the land. Led by BLM intern Kylie Stear, a graduate student at Boise State University, ICC crews completed a variety of projects, including habitat surveys, fencing maintenance, restoration planting, and trash cleanup. Idaho Conservation Crew repairing fence BLM internships provide students with the opportunity to gain direct experience in their field of study while leading ICC crews in meaningful conservation work. The BLM collaborated with the ICC and Northwest Youth Corps to provide internship opportunities throughout a four-year period from 2024 through 2028. Typical internships last 16 weeks but may be extended as project needs allow. This year, the BLM Boise District hired three interns to support work across the Snake River Plain, focusing on habitat inventory, exclosure repair, and monitoring for the threatened Slickspot peppergrass ( Lepidium papilliferum ). Their work benefits a wide variety of plant and wildlife species while supporting restoration efforts and other multiple-use activities throughout the Snake River Plain. Kylie Stear, BLM intern planting a seedling, helping to restore the landscape where the Range Fire had burned. We caught up with Kylie to hear about her internship experience. What did you enjoy most? “I enjoyed the mutual confidence-building between myself and the crews. I’m grateful for the opportunity to lead people who were interested in and dedicated to making a difference through surveying, conservation, and habitat monitoring. Hands-on work in the sagebrush-steppe fosters an appreciation for semi-arid ecosystems, and many of these crew members came from forest backgrounds, so it was a pleasure to share the value of desert landscapes.” What skills will you carry forward? “The ability to plan and organize fieldwork with a team to accomplish a common goal was both rewarding and highly transferable. Learning new information quickly, applying it to projects with short turnaround times, navigating mapping software, and communicating with partners outside the organization all came with a steep learning curve. I’m grateful for the confidence I’ve gained in each of those areas.” After working with the BLM for a year, how has your perspective on public lands changed? “I’ve come to value stewardship more than I did before working with the BLM. Proper land management supports not only ecosystems, but culture as well. The value, respect, and pride we have for our home is reflected in how we interact with the landscape. I’ve gained a deeper understanding of the responsibility we all share to care for public lands, whether through an organization like the BLM or as individuals. We each have the ability to make a difference, and it’s important that we do.” What are your plans after your internship? “I’ll be starting my master’s program at Boise State University in August. During my time with the BLM, I conducted habitat surveys for the rare and endemic Slickspot peppergrass . Now that I’ve spent a year becoming familiar with its habitat, I’ll shift my focus to studying the plant itself and helping develop a breeding program to support its conservation. Información básica sobre la vacuna contra la influenza (gripe) estacional Para todos 12 de nov. del 2026 English (US) Lo que debe saber Esta página proporciona información esencial sobre las vacunas contra la influenza (gripe) estacional, incluidos su propósito y efectividad. Todas las personas de 6 meses de edad o más —con raras excepciones— deberían vacunarse contra la influenza cada temporada. La vacunación es particularmente importante para las personas que tienen mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones graves por la influenza. Las personas con alergia al huevo pueden recibir cualquier vacuna (producida o no en huevo) que sea adecuada para su edad y estado de salud. La vacuna contra la influenza previene millones de casos de enfermedad y visitas al médico relacionadas con la influenza cada año. Beneficios de la vacunación contra la influenza La vacunación contra la influenza puede evitar que usted contraiga la enfermedad. La vacuna contra la influenza previene millones de casos de enfermedad y visitas al médico relacionadas con la influenza cada año. Por ejemplo, durante la temporada de influenza 2019-2020 , la última antes de la pandemia de COVID-19, se estima que la vacunación contra la influenza previno 7 millones de casos de la enfermedad y 3 millones de visitas médicas, 100 000 hospitalizaciones y 7000 muertes asociadas a la influenza en los Estados Unidos. Durante las temporadas en las que los virus de la influenza en la vacuna son similares a los que están en circulación, la vacuna ha demostrado que reduce el riesgo de tener que ir al médico con influenza entre un 40 y un 60 %. Las vacunas y las personas con alergias al huevo Las personas con alergia al huevo pueden recibir cualquier vacuna (producida o no en huevo) que sea adecuada para su edad y estado de salud. Seguir leyendo Las vacunas contra la influenza y las personas con alergias al huevo Por qué es importante vacunarse La influenza es una enfermedad potencialmente grave que puede causar la hospitalización y a veces incluso la muerte. Cada temporada de influenza es diferente y la enfermedad puede afectar a las personas de diferentes maneras, pero durante las temporadas de influenza típicas, millones de personas contraen la enfermedad, cientos de miles son hospitalizadas y entre miles y decenas de miles de personas mueren por causas relacionadas con la influenza. La influenza puede hacer que una persona se sienta mal durante algunos días y tenga que faltar al trabajo, a la escuela o a eventos familiares, o puede causar una enfermedad más grave. U.S. Department of Energy to Distribute First Amounts of HALEU to U.S. Advanced Reactor Developers The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today made conditional commitments to provide high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) to five U.S. nuclear developers to meet their near-term fuel needs. Energy.gov April 9, 2025 Estimated Read Time min WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today made conditional commitments to provide high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) to five U.S. nuclear developers to meet their near-term fuel needs. This first round of HALEU allocations brings innovative American nuclear technologies one step closer to commercialization and will expand the use of nuclear energy to deliver more secure, affordable, and reliable energy to the American people. “The Trump Administration is unleashing all sources of affordable, reliable and secure American energy – and this includes accelerating the deployment of advanced nuclear reactors,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said . “Allocating this HALEU material will help U.S. nuclear developers deploy their advanced reactors with materials sourced from secure supply chains, marking an important step forward in President Trump’s program to revitalize America’s nuclear sector.” Many advanced reactors will need HALEU to achieve smaller designs, longer operating cycles, and increased efficiencies over current technologies, but HALEU is not currently available from domestic suppliers. To help fill this gap, DOE created the HALEU allocation process for nuclear developers to request HALEU material from DOE sources, including material from the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA). DOE received HALEU requests from 15 companies. For this first round, DOE identified five of those companies that met prioritization criteria, with three of them requiring fuel delivery in 2025. The five companies that received conditional commitments are: • TRISO-X, LLC. • Kairos Power, LLC. • Radiant Industries, Inc. • Westinghouse Electric Company, LLC • TerraPower, LLC. The allocated HALEU supports both Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP) Pathway 1 award recipients, companies planning to demonstrate in the DOME test bed, along with some ARDP risk reduction awardees – reinforcing DOE’s commitment to our industry partnerships. As a next step, DOE will initiate the contracting process to allocate the material to the five companies, some of which could receive their HALEU as early as this fall. The allocation process is ongoing, and DOE plans to continue HALEU allocations to additional companies in the future. The first round of conditional commitments of HALEU were made through the HALEU Availability Program, which was established in 2020 to secure a domestic supply of HALEU for civilian domestic research, development, demonstration, and commercial use. Learn more about DOE’s HALEU Availability Program at HALEU Availability Program | Department of Energy . ### View Next Press Release U.S. Secretary of Energy Kicks Off Middle East Trip in UAE April 9, 2025 View Previous Press Release Energy Department Acts to Unleash American Coal by Strengthening Coal Technology and Securing Critical Mineral Supply Chains April 8, 2025 Media Inquiries: (202) 586-4940 or DOENews@hq.doe.gov Read more at the energy.gov Newsroom

pages.title: Searching the Seabed for Florida’s Ice Age Societies | National Geographic
pages.description: Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America.
pages.text: Searching the Seabed for Florida’s Ice Age Societies | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT Searching the Seabed for Florida’s Ice Age Societies Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America. Archaeologists are diving the coastline that stretches from Texas to Florida to find artifacts from tribes that once lived there thousands of years ago—like these arrowheads from McFadden Beach, just outside present-day Houston. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photo (Composite): Sepia Times/Universal Images Group, Getty Images; Melanie J. Stright, 1999 dissertation, U.S. Department of the Interior Minerals Management Service By Nicolás Rivero Published October 23, 2026 Five miles off Florida’s coast, in a sandy pit on the seafloor near a coral reef, archaeologist Morgan Smith picked up a stone tool someone dropped on dry land 7,000 years ago. It was December 2024, and Smith, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, was diving on an underwater mission to find signs of ancient human life. He sifted through 30 inches of sand and crushed seashells, down to a layer of blue-gray clay silt that could only have formed in a terrestrial environment. There, in this ancient, submerged dirt, he found a stone scraping tool the size of his hand. Digging deeper, he and one of his students also found an 8,500-year-old hunk of wood from a prehistoric tree. “Holy cow!” Smith recalls thinking. It was the first time anyone had found a stone tool buried in ancient dirt beneath this part of the ocean. Today, this spot is eight feet underwater. But millennia ago, after the last Ice Age, modern-day Florida’s western coastline extended around 100 miles further out. That’s the coastal landscape the first human beings in North America would have found when they arrived at least 15,000 years ago in what is today the coastal region of the southeastern U.S. Since then, sea levels have risen more than 300 feet. That now submerged land now holds clues about the lives of America’s earliest residents. With 100 miles of their former homelands now underwater, Ian Thompson, an archaeologist and the tribal historic preservation officer for the Choctaw Nation, thinks there are “significant early archaeological sites” throughout the region. Today, Thompson and Smith are among nearly a dozen scientists working on a new five-year project funded by the federal Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) to survey the seabed and find better ways to identify archaeological sites hidden beneath it. They hope their work will make it easier for researchers to piece together a picture of what life in this lost landscape looked like. “Thirty years ago, the challenge was: Can we find these sites?” said Jessica Cook Hale, an underwater archaeologist at Britain’s University of Bradford’s Submerged Landscapes Research Centre. “Now, the question is: What were people doing there?” The answer could change our understanding of how ancient humans survived the globe-spanning floods that followed the last Ice Age and even how and when people first came to the Americas. “These sites,” notes Sara Dailey-Smith, a partner on the MMA project representing the Chickasaw Nation, “could be lost pages of our history.” The MMA project is the biggest effort in history to identify where people might have lived across the 89 million submerged acres, from Texas to western Florida, that were once land. But the scientists are building on decades of research done by pioneering divers who have been searching for archaeological sites here since 1989. The team behind this work has spent the past two years analyzing sonar scans of the seafloor and sub-bottom profiles made using sound waves that show buried layers of sediment and rock. Learn about eligibility How do I apply? Learn how to apply How do I pay back my loan? Learn about payments What is the 504 loan program? The 504 loan program provides long-term, fixed rate financing for major fixed assets that promote business growth and job creation. Certified Development Companies (CDCs) are authorized by SBA to originate in collaboration with a senior lender a 504 loan, SBA’s community-based nonprofit partners who promote economic development within their communities. CDCs are certified and regulated by SBA. The maximum loan amount for a 504 loan is $5.5 million. Am I eligible? To be eligible for a 504 loan, your business must: Be an operating business Operate for profit Be located in the U.S. Be small under SBA size requirements Not be a type of ineligible business Other general eligibility standards include falling within SBA size guidelines, having qualified management expertise, a feasible business plan, good character and the ability to repay the loan. Loans cannot be made to businesses engaged in nonprofit, passive, or speculative activities. For additional information on eligibility criteria and loan application requirements, small businesses and lenders are encouraged to contact a Certified Development Company in their area. How do I use a 504 loan? A 504 loan can be used for a range of assets that promote business growth and job creation. These include the purchase or construction of: The purchase, construction or renovation of existing buildings or land Long-term machinery and equipment with a useful remaining life of a minimum of 10 years, including project-related AI-supported equipment or machinery for manufacturing products Consolidating debt under the conditions listed in 13 CFR 120.882 , paragraph (e) and Repaying or refinancing debt defined as “qualified debt” under 13 CFR 120.882 , paragraph (g) A 504 loan cannot be used for: Working capital or inventory Consolidating, repaying or refinancing debt that does not meet the definition of “qualified debt” under 13 CFR 120.882 , paragraphs (e) and (g) Speculation or investment in rental real estate How do I apply? 504 loans are available exclusively through Certified Development Companies (CDCs). Find a CDC in your area or contact your local SBA office to ensure you are dealing with a qualified lender. CDCs are uniquely qualified to understand 504 loan program regulations, and will help you navigate the lender channels to create your project financing. Find a CDC near you Find Certified Development Companies (CDCs) authorized to issue 504 loans. Find CDCs How do I pay back my 504 loan? Active loans Loan repayment terms vary according to several factors. Borrowers with active 504 loans can make payments through the Central Servicing Agent, usually by ACH monthly draws. Payments can also be made by wire. Repayment terms 10-, 20- and 25-year maturity terms are available. Interest rates Pegged to an increment above the current market rate for 10-year U.S. Treasury issues. Totals approximately 3% of the debt, rate may be financed with the loan For help with your account balance, due date, or any other questions regarding the specifics of your loan, contact your CDC. Purchased 504 debentures Borrowers with debenture-purchased 504 loans can create an account in the SBA Loan Portal to monitor their loan status and make payments.

pages.description: Home tests claim they can teach you about your health by testing your gut microbiome … but how accurate are their measurements?

Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/home-gut-microbiome-tests-give-varying-results Taking Measure Just a Standard Blog Home Gut Microbiome Tests Give Varying Results June 24, 2026 By: Stephanie Servetas Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email Stephanie Servetas is a microbiologist at NIST who studies the gut microbiome. Credit: Megan King/NIST Editor’s note: This blog post discusses the scientific study of fecal matter (aka poop). If that’s bothersome to you, you might want to skip this one (or at least not read it while eating). You may have heard about companies that claim they can give you lifestyle advice by analyzing a stool sample, similar to how you can decode your DNA with saliva. A team of microbiologists at NIST recently put these tests … well … to the test using precisely measured stool samples we already had in our labs. Microbiome Mysteries The gut microbiome is a collection of microbes — such as bacteria, fungi and viruses — that live in our gastrointestinal tract. The microbiome can’t be easily checked while it’s inside your body, but it can be analyzed from a stool sample. It’s important to understand just how challenging it is to learn about a person’s microbiome. You can’t just put a stool sample under a microscope and figure out what’s happening in the body. The reality is that preparing and studying a sample is a complex, multistep process. At any point, it’s easy to accidentally take a step that might affect the accuracy of your results, which we call introducing bias. Another significant challenge is that our gut microbiomes are very different from person to person, so there’s no “normal” gut microbiome that scientists have been able to pinpoint. In addition, the microbiome does not exist by itself in your stool — undigested food, bacteria, dead cells and other things also reside in a stool sample. Many companies offer gut microbiome tests that claim to help you learn more about your health. NIST experts put these tests to the test and found varying results. Credit: Shobujsk/Shutterstock A gut microbiome test is different from a medical test you may be accustomed to, such as a blood test. In an iron blood test, for example, physicians know what they’re looking for and how much they should find. They conduct the test and check if your results fall within a specific range. These tests have existed for many decades, with standardized methodologies for conducting them. Microbiome science, in contrast, is quite new. The field is only around 20 years old, and there’s still so much that researchers are learning about this complex and interesting part of our bodies. Microbiome researchers don’t have the technology and the research knowledge to say, “Yes, this is 100% what we were expecting to find in your microbiome.” Testing the Test In our recent study , we sent identical stool samples from one donor, which we’ve already studied and understand very well, to seven different microbiome test companies. This was an anonymous test, so the companies didn’t know they were being researched. The results we received were quite different, even though the companies received identical samples. One company, for example, marked a sample as having an “unhealthy” gut microbiome, while none of the other companies did. The likely reason for this is the bias issue I mentioned above. Different labs are handling samples differently, introducing varying levels of bias. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Cottonwood Field Office and Extreme Adventure Club Strengthen Youth Engagement Through Annual Float Trip on the Lower Salmon River Jul 31, 2026 Students reach the shore of the Lower Salmon River during their field trip with the University of Idaho’s Extreme Adventure Club. On July 21, the Bureau of Land Management’s Cottonwood Field Office, in close partnership with the University of Idaho’s Extreme Adventure Club, hosted 34 youth ages 8 to 14 for a full-day float down the Lower Salmon River. Traveling from Twin Bridges to the White Bird Gravel Pit, the event marked the third year of this coordinated effort to expand outdoor opportunities for local youth and strengthen community connections to public lands. Students rafting the Lower Salmon River. This annual float is the product of a strong and ongoing partnership between the BLM and the Extreme Adventure Club—an organization whose mission is to promote health and wellness within the community through educational events, programs, and presentations. By offering lifetime activity experiences to youth ages 8 to 14, the Extreme Adventure Club provides structured opportunities that complement the BLM’s commitment to public land stewardship, recreation access, and youth engagement. Employees from the BLM Cottonwood Field Office, staff from the USDA Forest Service, and several volunteers worked together to support the trip, rowing boats, teaching river skills, and ensuring a safe and memorable experience along one of Idaho’s most iconic river corridors. In addition to some enjoying their first rafting experience, many of the kids had the unique opportunity to practice rowing the BLM rafts themselves under the guidance of agency staff—an interactive lesson that helped build confidence, reinforce safe boating techniques, and offering an introduction to outdoor adventure that was both educational and exciting.Throughout the day, youth received hands-on lessons about river safety, responsible recreation, and the importance of public lands in local communities. The group also enjoyed swimming, jumping from boats, running rapids, and included a lunch stop at BLM's Skookumchuck Recreation Site. These moments of fun were paired with discussions about wildlife, land stewardship, and the outdoor opportunities available close to home. Students along the shores of the Lower Salmon River. The Office of Labor-Management Standards (OLMS) conducts compliance audits of all unions covered by the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 (LMRDA), and of Federal sector unions under the standards of conduct provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA). Compliance audits are designed to verify LMRDA or CSRA compliance, investigate potential violations of the law, and provide compliance assistance to help unions meet statutory requirements. The audits are based on a streamlined approach, using specialized records review and investigative techniques. At the conclusion of an OLMS audit, a closing letter is sent to the union describing the reporting deficiencies, recordkeeping violations, and internal control problems identified during the audit. The closing letters do not purport to be an exhaustive list of all possible problem areas since the audits are limited in scope. Audits of local unions and intermediate bodies are conducted under the Compliance Audit Program (CAP). Audits of national and international unions are conducted under International Compliance Audit Program (I-CAP) procedures. Audits are primarily conducted by OLMS investigators. Diagnóstico de la influenza 10 de mar. del 2026 English (US) Puntos clave La influenza (gripe) es una enfermedad respiratoria contagiosa que puede causar fiebre, tos, dolor de garganta, moqueo o congestión nasal, dolores corporales, dolor de cabeza, escalofríos o fatiga. Hay varias pruebas que pueden detectar los virus de la influenza. Aunque las pruebas son la única manera de saber si usted tiene la influenza, su proveedor de atención médica podría darle el diagnóstico con base en sus síntomas. Signos y síntomas a los que hay que estar atentos Su enfermedad respiratoria podría ser influenza si presenta signos o síntomas, tales como fiebre, tos, dolor de garganta, moqueo o congestión nasal, dolores corporales, dolor de cabeza, escalofríos o fatiga. Algunas personas también podrían tener vómitos y diarrea, aunque esto es más común en los niños. También se puede estar enfermo de influenza y tener síntomas respiratorios sin presentar fiebre. Los virus de la influenza generalmente causan enfermedad durante los meses más fríos del año. Sin embargo, también pueden causar enfermedad fuera de la temporada típica de influenza. Además, otros virus pueden causar también enfermedad respiratoria similar a la influenza. Por lo tanto, es imposible saber con certeza si usted tiene la influenza basándose solo en sus síntomas. Si su proveedor de atención médica necesita saberlo con certeza, hay pruebas de laboratorio que se pueden hacer. Diferentes tipos de pruebas de detección de la influenza Hay varias pruebas disponibles para detectar los virus de la influenza en muestras respiratorias. El tipo más común se llama "prueba de diagnóstico rápido de la influenza (RIDT, por sus siglas en inglés)". La forma en que las pruebas de diagnóstico rápido de la influenza funcionan es detectando las partes del virus (antígenos) que provocan una respuesta inmunitaria. Algunas pruebas de diagnóstico rápido de la influenza están aprobadas por la FDA y disponibles para uso en el hogar, incluidas aquellas capaces de detectar los virus de la influenza A y B, así como el SARS-CoV-2 (el virus que causa el COVID-19) en muestras tomadas de las vías respiratorias superiores. Estas pruebas pueden dar resultados dentro de aproximadamente 10 a 15 minutos, pero podrían no ser tan precisas como otras pruebas de influenza. Por lo tanto, aunque su prueba rápida dé negativo, aún podría tener la influenza. Otro tipo de pruebas son los "análisis moleculares rápidos" que pueden detectar el material genético de los virus de la influenza. Estos análisis dan resultados en 15-20 minutos y son más precisos que las pruebas de diagnóstico rápido de la influenza. Además de las pruebas de diagnóstico rápido de la influenza y los análisis moleculares rápidos, hay varias pruebas de influenza más precisas que están disponibles; estas deben hacerse en laboratorios especializados, como laboratorios hospitalarios y de salud pública. Estas pruebas incluyen pruebas de reacción en cadena de la polimerasa con transcripción inversa (RT-PCR) y ensayos de inmunofluorescencia. Todas estas pruebas requieren que un proveedor de atención médica tome una muestra de la nariz o la parte de atrás de la garganta con un bastoncito de algodón y la envíe a un laboratorio para su análisis. Una vez en el laboratorio, los resultados pueden tardar de una a varias horas. Pruebas de detección de la influenza para hacerse en casa Los CDC no cuentan con directrices específicas para el uso de pruebas de detección de la influe

pages.description: OpenStreetMap is a map of the world, created by people like you and free to use under an open license.
pages.text: Peter Elderson's Diary | Getting rid of source tags of an ancient mass import in Nederland | OpenStreetMap Select Language Loading... Close Peter Elderson's Diary Getting rid of source tags of an ancient mass import in Nederland Posted by Peter Elderson on 16 November 2026 in English . History In 2010, a paper map by 3dShapes was digitized and imported, to map landuse in Nederland. The import project was well conducted and properly documented in the OSM-wiki. This was a major step in filling in the space on OSM. Some problems remained after import, to be dealt with later. For instance, where trees had been planted in multiple rows, it was imported as an orchard. As a result, our motorways were suddenly lined with orchards, on OSM-based maps. This has been fixed by organized mappings. Another example: the paper map had a tile grid of thin black lines. These lines were seen as cut lines, resulting in unnecessary and awkward splits of the imported areas. The import procedure did detect this problem, but couldn’t automate a fix, so this was left to the future mappers. It took 15 years before a crazy mapper got rid of this in a solo project lasting 2 months. Guess who? The issue Not much of a problem, more of an annoyance, really: All polygons were tagged with “source=3dShapes”. A significant part of the polygons still carry this source tag. Many polygons have not been touched since import; many others have been edited but kept the original source tags; and many have been significantly altered or replaced thereby losing the original source tag. As a result, the tag is now generally meaningless. It only tells you that the former 3dShapes donated their map, but it tells you nothing about the current size, shape, object type, and tagging. These can be from unaltered to completely different. The current consensus is that source tags should not be attached to objects, but to changesets. Why not just mass remove this outdated source tag? Mass remove the 3dShapes source tag? Re Attribution: 3dShapes attribution is in the Wiki import pages and in the contributor list for Nederland. No need to keep it in every single imported object. Re History: Where history has been preserved, the v1 user (creator) is 3dShapes, even when the source tag is removed. Re Signal function: Some mappers (me included) remove the 3dShape source tag after significant edits of the polygon. If all mappers did that, the tag would signify untouched 3dShapes polygons that probably need checking and editing. But many more mappers just ignore the source tag, even when splitting or completely reshaping and retagging the element. So the signal function is lost. It is true that the 3dShapes tag combined with the history is significant. But you don’t need the 3dShapes source tag for that signal, just the history! To illustrate: There are MapRoulette challenges based on the presence of the source=3dShapes tag. The challenges contain enormous amounts of unordered objects, many of which have already been edited at some point. Will never be completed. A IMO much better method is what I used for another old import: AND road import. I selected highways having nodes that were last touched by the import user. You could copy this method: select polygons having nodes that were last touched by user 3dShapes. This still finds lots of already edited polygons, but chances are they still need fixing. Because: 1. many edits just touch one side of the polygon; 2. In Nederland, hardly anything remains exactly the same for 15 years, so nodes untouched for 15 years are outdated anyway. And it does not need the totally tainted tag, making it completely redundant. Discussion Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

pages.title: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: César Jáuregui Moreno is accused of allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April.
pages.text: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Ex-prosecutor charged with treason in Mexico over US drug raid 21 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Patrick Jackson Getty Images César Jáuregui Moreno (pictured) was arrested over the weekend Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation. César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year. The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers. Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations. The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday. A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports. Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country. She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached. The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine. Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said. At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities". US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region. pages.title: The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? | National Geographic
pages.description: From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis.
pages.text: The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? | National Geographic During the Little Ice Age, the Northern Hemisphere experienced long stretches of temperatures so cold that crops failed and rivers froze—like the Scheldt River, depicted here outside of Antwerp, Belgium, in a 1593 oil painting by Lucas van Valckenborch. Photograph by incamerastock, Alamy Stock Photo Premium ENVIRONMENT The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Little Ice Age was not a true ice age—average cooling was probably only in the order of 0.5 degrees Celsius , or 1 degree Fahrenheit—nor was it consistently cold. Dagomar Degroot, associate professor of environmental history at Georgetown University and author of The Frigid Golden Age has referred to the era as a series of “little little ice ages.” Although some researchers argue it may have begun earlier, NASA defines the Little Ice Age as beginning around 1550 and consisting of three cold peaks—around 1650, 1770 and 1850—interspersed with relative warm intervals. ( Why cold weather doesn't mean climate change is fake .) Scientists are still working out exactly what caused the Little Ice Age too. Theories range from decreased solar activity to increased volcanic eruptions , to the genocide of Indigenous populations in North America , which allowed forests to replace agricultural land, in the process removing about seven billion tons of carbon from the atmosphere. A 2022 study argued that the initial trigger was, counterintuitively, a surge of extremely warm water flowing north from the tropics in the late 1300s, which flushed Arctic ice into the North Atlantic. Widespread impacts Whatever the cause, the consequences of the Little Ice Age have rippled through history , although to what extent is controversial. Certainly, cold weather enabled Charles X Gustav of Sweden to march his troops across a frozen strait to capture the Danish island of Funen in 1658 , and made it possible for French troops to seize a Dutch fleet that had frozen into the ice in 1795—an event described as being the only time in history men on horseback captured a fleet of ships . Fear and anxiety at repeated crop failures prompted a surge of “witch trials” and anti-Semitism in Europe. ( Which U.S. cities will still be livable in a world altered by climate change? ) Less definitively, the Little Ice Age may have played a role in the collapse of the Ming Dynasty in China , partly as a result of food shortages leading to peasant uprisings. The drop in temperatures and a simultaneous growth in ice cover on land and sea may have contributed to the disappearance of Norse colonies from Greenland . It has even been postulated that the unique sound of Stradivarius violins results from the wood that Antonio Stradivari used being denser than usual because of the cold . pages.title: My Research Is Working Toward a Pain-Free Mammogram Alternative | NIST Lock
pages.description: A NIST researcher is working toward a future screening test for breast cancer that’s painless and highly effective.
pages.text: My Research Is Working Toward a Pain-Free Mammogram Alternative | NIST Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/my-research-working-toward-pain-free-mammogram-alternative Taking Measure Just a Standard Blog My Research Is Working Toward a Pain-Free Mammogram Alternative May 20, 2026 By: Kathryn Keenan Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email NIST researcher Kathryn Keenan tests a low-field MRI machine adapted to capture breast imagery. The long-term goal of this research is to create a pain-free, accurate alternative to mammograms. Credit: M. Rosen/Mass General Brigham Department of Radiology At some point in my teenage years, I became aware that when I grew up, I’d have to get a mammogram, and it was clear that it would hurt. If you’re a woman over 40 (or you’ve talked to women over 40 about this topic), you probably know that this annual screening requirement for all women is uncomfortable at best and can be painful. Can you imagine, a woman who lives into her 80s may have to undergo this test 40 or more times throughout her life?! But it is a lifesaving test that all women (and some men) need . Now, I’m a medical imaging researcher, and I know that a less painful alternative to breast cancer screening is possible within my lifetime. I have a goal some might consider outrageous — to create a viable alternative to mammograms that is pain-free, highly accurate and can save even more lives than mammograms currently do. Challenges of Mammography Mammograms use low-dose X-rays to take a picture of the inside of the breast. The breast must be compressed to increase the image quality, but that compression makes it uncomfortable. Mammograms are incredibly important tests that have saved many lives . Right now, they are the best option we have to detect and treat breast cancer early, and everyone eligible for mammograms should prioritize getting them. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t drawbacks. First, mammograms can miss up to 35% of breast cancers. On the other end of the spectrum, mammograms also can give false positives up to 14.4% of the time . This can mean extra tests, including painful biopsies, for patients to rule out breast cancer. This risk is especially high for the up to half of women over age 40 who have dense breast tissue . Breasts are made up of two types of tissue — dense tissue and fatty tissue. Women with dense breasts have more dense tissue. Dense tissue is normal and nothing to be concerned about, but dense tissue makes mammography more challenging and can lead to false positives . Mammograms are vital to women’s health, but they do have drawbacks — including discomfort. But a NIST researcher is working toward a viable alternative that can be even more accurate and less painful. Credit: Frame Stock Footage/Shutterstock Low-Field MRI and Breast Cancer Screening My research focuses on lower-strength magnetic-field equipment, known as low-field MRI . Unlike a traditional MRI, which is a large, expensive machine, low-field MRI machines are smaller and less costly. That’s because they use a weaker magnetic field to capture an image. The weaker magnetic field means the images are not as clear as traditional MRI. My goal is to use this same technology to create a way to screen patients for breast cancer. Breast imaging with traditional MRI can be done now, and it does not require the breast compression used for mammography. But MRI is expensive and is often reserved for patients who need follow-up testing. With low-field MRI, this option could be available to many more patients. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Sharing the Spirit of America: A Celebration on the Snake River Canyon Rim Jul 9, 2026 The Bureau of Land Management joined the Idaho State Historical Society, America 250 in Idaho, Jerome County, and the Snake River Canyons Park Board—along with many community partners—yesterday on the north rim of the Snake River Canyon for Sharing the Spirit of America , a global, simultaneous reading of the Declaration of Independence. With Shoshone Falls as a dramatic backdrop, Idaho added its voice to coordinated readings across all 50 states, each of the five Territories, DC, Midway, Wake, Palmyra and all seven continents in honor of the Declaration’s first public readings 250 years ago. Participants pose with the Great American Expedition flag which helps highlight the people, places, and stories that define America’s public lands heritage. Even in mid‑construction, the future overlook proved a powerful and symbolic setting. Years of shared vision and collaboration among the BLM, Jerome County, the Snake River Canyons Park Board, and partners like Chobani and Idaho Power are bringing this long‑imagined project to life. Once complete, the overlook will expand public access, enhance heritage tourism, and foster deeper appreciation for one of Idaho’s most iconic landscapes. Even today, its emerging form reflects what communities can accomplish when they work together. Decades in the making, this new overlook shows off the beauty and majesty of the Snake River Canyon and provided a fitting backdrop for this America 250 event. Public lands provided a fitting landscape for reflecting on the meaning of freedom and the legacy of 1776. The canyon’s sweeping geology, shaped by time and natural force, reminds us that history is not separate from the places we stand—it lives in our rivers, our valleys, and our public spaces. America 250 in Idaho encourages communities to “do history” in meaningful ways: to support storytelling, preserve places that matter, and connect Idahoans to the lands that help tell the nation’s story. Yesterday’s gathering embodied that mission, linking the principles of the American Revolution with the modern stewardship of shared landscapes. Posing with the Expedition Flag are (L to R) Kelsey Brizendine (USWFS), Samantha Storms (Idaho Power), Daryl Ferguson (BLM Archaeologist), Heather Tiel-Nelson (DOI Communications), and Lisa Cresswell (BLM Shoshone Field Manager). The afternoon culminated in a collective reading of the Declaration of Independence by the BLM Idaho State Director, the Idaho Secretary of State, a Jerome County Commissioner, and an Idaho State University history student. As participants joined together in the closing lines, the moment echoed the first public readings of 1776—acts of courage and shared purpose that once rang out across Philadelphia, Trenton, and Easton, and yesterday resonated once more across the canyon rim. Toward the end of the ceremony, these four read a section of the Declaration of Independence, exactly 250 years to the day after it was first presented publicly on July 8, 1776. Left to right in order of reading: BLM Idaho State Director Meagan Conry, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, Idaho’s Jerome County Commissioner Charlie Howell, ISU student Andrew Wilsey. The final sentence was read aloud by the entire audience. As the United States celebrates 250 years of independence and the BLM marks its 80th year, Sharing the Spirit of America honored both our nation’s past and the partnerships shaping our shared

Using all 3 will keep your clients’ data safer. Cybercriminals target tax professionals because you are custodians of highly sensitive client data. They attempt to steal your client's personal financial information so they can create fraudulent tax returns and claim fake refunds. Report suspected identity theft or data loss Your clients If your clients need assistance preventing, reporting, or recovering from identity theft, review our information for: Individuals Businesses You or your firm If you or your firm are the victim of data theft, immediately : Report it to your local stakeholder liaison Liaisons will notify IRS Criminal Investigation and others within the agency on your behalf. Speed is critical. If reported quickly, the IRS can take steps to block fraudulent returns in your clients’ names and will assist you through the process. Get information on how to report victim information to state tax agencies. Visit the Federation of Tax Administrators Report a Data Breach to find state contact information. Find more information at Data theft information for tax professionals . Protect your clients and prevent data loss You are the first line of defense against identity theft. You must be alert and on guard at all times. In addition to trying to steal client data, thieves may try to steal your identity as well, using your PTINs, EFINs and CAF numbers to file fraudulent returns or steal even more information. Know your responsibilities Federal law requires you to create, implement and maintain an information security plan to protect client data, no matter the size of your firm . It sets the information security framework for federal agencies. It also produced this document to provide small businesses with an overview of those steps to security data. Note: The IRS can’t recommend security products. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) administers the law and created the Safeguards Rule. Tratamiento de la influenza 23 de abr. del 2026 English (US) Vistazo general Si se enferma de influenza, una opción de tratamiento pueden ser los medicamentos antivirales contra la influenza. Los medicamentos antivirales pueden hacer que la enfermedad sea más leve y acortar el periodo en el que está enfermo. También pueden prevenir algunas complicaciones por la influenza, como la neumonía. Los medicamentos antivirales contra la influenza son más eficaces si se inician de forma temprana, idealmente entre los dos días de la aparición de los síntomas de la influenza. Información general sobre el tratamiento Los antivirales contra la influenza son medicamentos recetados (pastillas, solución líquida, polvo para inhalar o solución intravenosa) que combaten la influenza en sus vías respiratorias. Los medicamentos antivirales no se venden sin receta médica. Solo puede conseguirlos en una farmacia si tiene una receta de su médico o proveedor de atención médica. Los medicamentos antivirales son diferentes de los antibióticos, los cuales combaten las infecciones bacterianas y no funcionan contra los virus, como la influenza. La mayoría de las personas con influenza tienen una enfermedad leve y no necesitan atención médica ni medicamentos antivirales. Si presenta síntomas de influenza, en la mayoría de los casos debería permanecer en su casa y evitar el contacto con otras personas, excepto para recibir atención médica. Seguir leyendo Signos y síntomas de la influenza Sin embargo, si tiene síntomas de influenza y tiene mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones , está muy enfermo de influenza o está preocupado por su enfermedad, comuníquese con su proveedor de atención médica de inmediato. Los CDC recomiendan iniciar el tratamiento lo antes posible para las personas que tienen influenza o se sospecha que la tienen, y corren mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones graves por la influenza, como las personas con asma, diabetes o enfermedades cardiacas. Seguir leyendo Personas con mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones por la influenza La mayoría de las personas que no tienen grandes riesgos de presentar complicaciones por la influenza y que contraen la enfermedad no necesitan un tratamiento con medicamentos antivirales. Los medicamentos antivirales pueden ayudar a tratar la influenza Los medicamentos antivirales deberían iniciarse lo antes posible cuando aparecen los síntomas. Los estudios muestran que el tratamiento de la influenza con medicamentos antivirales es más eficaz si se inicia dentro de los dos días después de la aparición de los síntomas de influenza, y puede aliviar los síntomas y reducir el tiempo en que está enfermo en aproximadamente un día. Comenzar el tratamiento antiviral poco después de que comiencen los síntomas también puede ayudar a reducir algunas complicaciones de la influenza. Sin embargo, incluso si el tratamiento se inicia después, puede ser útil, especialmente si la persona tiene una condición médica que aumenta su riesgo o está muy enfermo de influenza (por ejemplo, los pacientes hospitalizados). Siga las instrucciones de su médico para tomar estos medicamentos. Lo que no debe hacer Los antibióticos no sirven para tratar la influenza Los antibióticos no funcionan contra los virus. Cuando los antibióticos no son necesarios, no ayudan y sus efectos secundarios pueden hacer daño. Los efectos secundarios varían de reacciones leves, como un sarpullido, a problemas de salud más graves. Estos problemas pueden incluir reaccio

pages.title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were killed on a surfing trip in an apparent botched robbery.
pages.text: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico 17 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Will Grant , BBC's Mexico Correspondent and Joel Guinto How a harrowing trial of two murdered Australian surfers ended in a guilty verdict A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each. The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico. The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them". The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. pages.title: A Soviet sea, killed by an obsession with 'white gold' | National Geographic
pages.description: In 1990, National Geographic went to the Soviet Union to report on one of the worst environmental disasters of the 20th century: the shrinking of the Aral Sea.
pages.text: A Soviet sea, killed by an obsession with 'white gold' | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT FROM THE VAULT A Soviet sea, killed by an obsession with 'white gold' In 1990, National Geographic went to the Soviet Union to report on one of the worst environmental disasters of the 20th century: the shrinking of the Aral Sea. From the rusting deck of the boat he captained for years, Dzhetpisbai Ibragimov surveys a sandy waste once part of the great Aral Sea. By William S. Ellis Photographs by David C. Turnley Published April 21, 2026 This story originally published in the February 1990 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . The mighty inland sea lies stricken now, caught in the grip of some evil chemistry as its waters dry to salt and blow away as noxious dust to strike the people with illness and death. It has never happened before within the time frame of a single generation, the disappearance of such a large body of water; but the Soviet Union's Aral Sea, once larger in area than any of the Great Lakes save Superior, is vanishing from the face of the earth. As the waters continue to recede, final destruction of the Aral—26,000 square miles in 1960—could occur before another 30 years have passed. The desiccation is taking place not only at a rapid pace but also with stealth, and in silence: the way a stallion plunges his muzzle into a bucket of water and drains it. Wide concern was late in coming and was delayed until now, when there is little that can be done to save the sea. Before the emergence of Mikhail Gorbachev as the head of the Soviet government and his policy of glasnost , or openness, the calamity was not widely reported or even discussed in the Soviet Union. Rather, it was blurred to the public eye by the myopia of previous regimes. Ecology was not a primary concern. The well-being of a huge body of water sitting in the desert wastes of the Soviet Central Asian republics of Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan was subordinate to the good of the state, to the successful fulfillment of plans and quotas. And so it was decreed in 1918 that waters of the two great rivers feeding the Aral would be drawn off to irrigate millions of acres for cotton production. There was a Soviet obsession to be self-sufficient in cotton. In 1937 the Soviet Union became a net exporter of what planners had come to refer to as "white gold." But the cost of that self-sufficiency and of export profits would be nothing less than one of the most extraordinary violations of the environment in modern times. ( Read our May 2026 feature about the Aral Sea—now. ) The Aral Sea was worth sacrificing if the vast Central Asian desert could be made to bloom, Soviet experts believed when construction began on the 850-mile Kara Kum Canal in 1954. In the next 30 years several other large diversions were built to irrigate more cotton, rice, and melons. Eventually the Syr and Amu, Soviet Central Asia's largest rivers, would be emptied of virtually all the water they carried down from the Pamirs and the Tian Shan, cutting inflow to the lake to almost nothing. This map is from the 1990 article. NGS Cartographic Division "I doubt if there has ever been an environmental problem of this magnitude," said Philip P. Micklin, a leading authority on the Aral Sea and a professor of geography at Western Michigan University. "Certainly as a regional problem affecting 35 million people, it is unprecedented." For ten thousand years the Aral has drawn its life from those two rivers, the 1,578-mile-long Amu Darya and the 1,370-mile-long Syr Darya. In classical times they were called the Oxus and the Jaxartes, but by whatever name they are streams of strength and character, celebrated in verse and in the rich history of the times when Tatar horsemen rode the dry steppes. The rivers come down from the mountain ranges to the southeast, flowing north to the Aral, and the routes they follow through deserts called the Kyzyl Kum and Kara Kum

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Nine Miles of Prevention: The Fuel Break that turned the Fire Jun 24, 2026 The Pothole South fuel break helped to stop the 2026 Sailor Cap fire When the fire first ignited deep within the Saylor Creek Range in south-central Idaho, its rapid spread was immediate and alarming. Driven by winds pushing it east‑southeast, the flames tore through miles of grasslands dotted with scattered pockets of brush. Before long, the fire had grown to 8,292 acres, burning across 2,589 acres of BLM‑managed land, 213 acres of State land, and 5,490 acres of Military property. As crews mobilized, U.S. Wildland Fire Service firefighter Chase Krapf approached the scene and witnessed something remarkable. A towering smoke column rose high above the desert—until, in an instant, it collapsed. The head of the fire had reached the Pothole South fuel break. Stretching approximately nine miles with a 275‑foot treatment area on both sides of the road, the Pothole South fuel break covers about 603 acres. Roughly 151 of those acres lay directly within the fire perimeter. Years of strategic work were being put to the test in a single, critical moment. The fuel break had been carefully built over multiple seasons, beginning in the fall of 2016. Vegetation was first removed through chemical applications, followed by additional treatments and seedbed preparation in the spring of 2017. That same spring, crews mowed standing dead vegetation and applied another round of herbicide to keep the corridor clear. In the fall of 2017, stabilizer wheatgrass was drill‑seeded to establish a low‑profile, fire‑resistant plant community. Winters of 2018 and 2019 brought aerial seedings of forage kochia, a hardy species known for slowing fire behavior. Additional chemical applications in 2019 and 2021 reduced invasive annuals, and maintenance mowing in 2022, 2023, and 2024 ensured the break remained effective and open. All of that effort paid off. The moment the fire hit the Pothole South fuel break, its behavior changed dramatically. The advancing flame front lost intensity, the towering smoke column laid down, and firefighters were able to safely and effectively engage. What could have been a fast‑running, difficult‑to‑contain wildfire instead slowed, allowing suppression resources to halt its forward progression. And in addition to the operational success, the financial impact was significant. By stopping the fire at the fuel break and reducing the need for extended aviation support, the U.S. WFS avoided potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars in suppression costs. For comparison, last week’s Median Fire required roughly 5.5 hours of retardant‑dropping aviation time—nearly $400,000 in costs alone. The effectiveness of the Pothole South fuel break illustrates how proactive fuels management doesn’t just protect lives and landscapes—it also protects budgets. The fire’s footprint tells one story. The fuel break tells another. Through sustained investment, strategic design, and ongoing maintenance, the Pothole South fuel break functioned exactly as intended—protecting the landscape, aiding firefighters, and preventing a dangerous wildfire from growing even larger. It stands as a clear example of how proactive fuels management pays off on every front: safety, effectiveness, and substantial cost savings. pages.text: Cuándo esperar su reembolso si reclamó el Crédito tributario por ingreso del trabajo o el Crédito tributario adicional por hijos | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Cuándo esperar su reembolso si reclamó el Crédito tributario por ingreso del trabajo o el Crédito tributario adicional por hijos English Español 中文 (简体) 中文 (繁體) 한국어 Русский Tiếng Việt Kreyòl ayisyen Más en Créditos y deducciones (en inglés) Familia, dependientes y estudiantes (en inglés) Crédito tributario por ingreso del trabajo Asistente calificador para el EITC Quién califica para el EITC Hijo o pariente calificado para el EITC Tablas de ingreso del trabajo y del crédito Cómo reclamar el EITC Cuándo debe esperar su reembolso si reclamó el EITC o el Crédito tributario adicional por hijos Crédito tributario por hijos Créditos tributarios por estudios (en inglés) Créditos y deducciones para energía limpia y vehículos (en inglés) Créditos y deducciones de individuos Créditos y deducciones para negocios y trabajadores por cuenta propia Si reclamó el Crédito tributario por ingreso del trabajo ( EITC , por sus siglas en inglés) o el Crédito tributario adicional por hijos ( ACTC , por sus siglas en inglés) (en inglés) , puede esperar obtener su reembolso para el 3 de marzo si: Usted presenta su declaración en línea Usted elige obtener su reembolso por depósito directo No encontramos problemas con su declaración Sin embargo, algunos contribuyentes pueden ver sus reembolsos unos días antes. Consulte Dónde está mi Reembolso para ver su fecha de reembolso personalizada. Dónde está mi Reembolso debe mostrar un estado actualizado para el 22 de febrero para la mayoría de los primeros solicitantes de EITC/ACTC . Además, es posible que su institución financiera necesite tiempo para aceptar su depósito directo o emitir una tarjeta de débito. Muchas instituciones no tramitan pagos los fines de semana o días feriados. Por lo tanto, si presenta su declaración temprano, tenga en cuenta que los días feriados federales y locales (en inglés) pueden afectar qué tan pronto obtenga su reembolso. Por qué retenemos su reembolso Conforme a la ley, no podemos emitir los reembolsos de EITC o ACTC antes de mediados de febrero. Esto incluye su reembolso completo, no solo la parte relacionada con el crédito que reclamó en su declaración de impuestos. Si reclama el EITC o ACTC , es posible que necesitemos más información de usted sobre su declaración. Si lo hacemos, le enviaremos una carta. Cómo rastrear su reembolso Verifique el estado de su reembolso en: Su cuenta en línea Dónde está mi reembolso Aplicación móvil IRS2 Go Actualizamos estas aplicaciones una vez al día, usualmente durante la noche. Esto significa que no hay necesidad de verificar el estado con más frecuencia. Recursos Reembolsos Page Last Reviewed or Updated: 25-Sep-2026 Share Facebook Twitter Linkedin Print

pages.description: Guía sobre qué hacer si se enferma.
pages.text: Influenza: qué hacer si se enferma | Influenza (Flu) | CDC Ir al contenido del sitio Ir a la búsqueda Un sitio oficial del Gobierno de Estados Unidos Así es como usted puede verificarlo Los sitios web oficiales usan .gov Un sitio web .gov pertenece a una organización oficial del Gobierno de Estados Unidos. Comparta información sensible sólo en sitios web oficiales y seguros. Influenza: qué hacer si se enferma 30 de ago. del 2024 English (US) Lo que debe saber La mayoría de las personas con influenza tienen una enfermedad leve y no necesitan atención médica ni medicamentos antivirales. Si presenta síntomas de influenza, en la mayoría de los casos debería permanecer en su casa y evitar el contacto con otras personas, excepto para recibir atención médica. Si tiene signos de advertencia de una emergencia correspondiente a la influenza, debería ir a la sala de emergencias. Medidas fundamentales que debe tomar cuando se enferma Si tiene síntomas de influenza y pertenece a un grupo con mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones graves relacionadas con esta enfermedad, o si está muy enfermo o preocupado sobre su enfermedad, comuníquese con su proveedor de atención médica. Ciertas personas tienen mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones graves relacionadas con la influenza (como los niños pequeños, las personas de 65 años o más, las mujeres embarazadas y las personas con ciertas condiciones médicas). Si usted pertenece a un grupo con mayor riesgo y presenta síntomas de influenza, comuníquese con su médico al inicio de la enfermedad. Recuérdele su estado de mayor riesgo de influenza. Los CDC recomiendan que las personas con mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones graves relacionadas con la influenza reciban un tratamiento antiviral lo antes posible, porque el beneficio es mayor si el tratamiento se empieza dentro de los 2 días del inicio de la enfermedad. Seguir leyendo Personas con mayor riesgo de presentar complicaciones por la influenza Cómo decidir si una visita a la sala de emergencias es necesaria si tiene una enfermedad leve La sala de emergencias debe ser usada por personas que están muy enfermas. Usted no debe ir a la sala de emergencias si solo tiene una enfermedad leve. Si tiene signos de advertencia de una emergencia correspondiente a la influenza, debería ir a la sala de emergencias. Si presenta síntomas de influenza y tiene mayor riesgo de complicaciones graves o le preocupa su enfermedad, llame a su proveedor de atención médica para pedirle consejos. Medicamentos para tratar la influenza Hay medicamentos que su médico podría recetar para tratar la influenza, llamados "antivirales". Estos medicamentos pueden hacer que se mejore más rápido y también pueden prevenir complicaciones graves. Seguir leyendo Tratamiento de la influenza con medicamentos antivirales Video en baja resolución Cantidad de tiempo recomendada para que se quede en casa cuando está enfermo Puede retomar sus actividades habituales cuando, por al menos 24 horas, se cumplan estos dos criterios: sus síntomas mejoran en general, y no ha tenido fiebre (sin estar tomando medicamentos antifebriles). Después de cumplir con estos dos criterios, hay algunas precauciones adicionales que se pueden tomar para proteger a los demás de las enfermedades respiratorias. Seguir leyendo Prevención de la propagación de virus respiratorios si está enfermo Notas Las personas con influenza son más contagiosas durante los primeros 3 días de la enfermedad. Algunas personas, como los niños pequeños y las personas con el sistema inmunitario debilitado, pueden ser contagiosas durante periodos más largos. No todas las personas con influenza tendrán fiebre. Las personas con un caso presunto o confirmado de influenza que no tengan fiebre deberían quedarse en casa y no ir a trabajar por al menos 5 días después del inicio de los síntomas. pages.title: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: The man, a Mexican firefighter, looked "nervous" as he tried to leave Cologne Airport, officials say.
pages.text: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport 15 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paulin Kola German Customs Not all the the snakes and lizards were alive, officials said A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes. Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport. They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase. They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks. "My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office. Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul. The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance. He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul. As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany. "Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said. Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico , were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport. They were destined for private buyers in Germany. pages.title: Can the Aral Sea be reborn? | National Geographic
pages.description: A generation ago, the vanishing of the Aral Sea became global shorthand for environmental desolation. Today the region has become a test bed for a resilient future.
pages.text: Can the Aral Sea be reborn? | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT Can the Aral Sea be reborn? A generation ago, the vanishing of the Aral Sea became global shorthand for environmental desolation. Today the region has become a test bed for a resilient future. A thermal spring, visited by locals for its reputed healing properties, bubbles up through the otherwise parched lake bed of the former Aral Sea in Kazakhstan. By Jeff Wise Photographs by Anush Babajanyan Published April 22, 2026 Listen to this story See more of our narrated audio articles here Audio Timeline Slider: Use the left or right arrow keys to decrease or increase the slider value. Play audio 15 15 Audio Unmuted. Mute Volume Slider: Use the left or right arrow keys to decrease or increase the slider value. 0:00 / 0:00 Sign in or subscribe to hear the full story It was the first human-made ecological disaster of the modern era. In 1960, the Aral Sea was the world’s fourth largest lake, a rich and productive ecosystem teeming with carp, bream, and other species—by one estimate, it provided a sixth of all fish consumed in the Soviet Union. Hundreds of feet deep and hundreds of miles across, the sea was a world unto itself for the people who lived and fished on its shores and for the sailors who crossed it. But change was coming. In 1968, Pravda, the official state newspaper of the Soviet Union, carried a story with an astonishing prophecy. This world would soon vanish, it said. Already the water level had started to fall, and it would fall further, its edges creeping away from the fishing towns on its shores, the lake bed changing to desert. By the turn of the century, “essentially, the Aral Sea will no longer exist.” There was no magic behind the prophecy—just math. In the preceding years, Soviet officials had built large-scale irrigation projects that diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, the rivers that fed the Aral Sea, into cotton production. Without their inflow, there was nothing to replace the water lost naturally through evaporation. For a brief time, the region enjoyed the best of both worlds: the lake, with its productive fisheries and mild climate, and the cotton industry, with the hard cash it earned. But as the rivers turned away, the lake shrank and shrank to less than 10 percent of its mid-century footprint, leaving behind a salt-encrusted desert. At the end of a day of picking cotton, workers line up to have their harvests weighed. Cotton is a major part of Uzbekistan’s economy, employing a quarter of its workforce, and the irrigation necessary to sustain it is the main reason little water reaches the Aral Sea anymore. The prophecy had been duly engineered: The Aral Sea as such no longer existed. “From an environmental perspective, it was a huge mistake,” says Bulat Yessekin, an environmental policy expert who spent decades working on Central Asian water access issues with international nonprofit groups. ( In 1990, National Geographic went to report on the shrinking of the Aral Sea, one of the worst environmental disasters of the 20th century. ) Today the Aral Sea stands not only as a worldwide symbol of catastrophe but also as the first domino to fall in a freshwater crisis. Iran’s Lake Urmia has also shrunk over the past half century by 90 percent, as has Lake Chad in Central Africa. In the United States, the Great Salt Lake in Utah has become so salty because of water loss that its brine shrimp are at risk of dying out. All these crises are tied together with the pressures of human population growth and climate change. But some conservationists are now looking to the fate of the Aral Sea and asking another question: If humanity can create ecological disaster, can we also undo it? The blunt answer is that we don’t know, and finding the solution will take time. None of these problems sprang up overnight.
